Industry News: Christopher Nolan and Guillermo del Toro Break Down ‘The Odyssey’ Monsters and AI’s Limitations with Production VFX Supervisor Andrew Jackson

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With “The Odyssey,” Christopher Nolan ventured into the realm of fantasy for the first time, realizing a time of towering monsters, swirling whirlpools, and apparent magic.
  • Industry observers note that “What’s essential is having the visual effects team be part of the main unit through prep, through the shoot, everything — and not treating you guys as somebody that’s going to come on afterwards and add to the film,” Nolan said, speaking with Jackson during a panel following a Visual Effects Society screening of “The Odyssey” at the IMAX auditorium of AMC Theatres’ Universal Cinema location in Los Angeles.
  • “What I’ve found through the years is to treat the effects as a remedial thing that is separate from everything is a big mistake,” del Toro added.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With “The Odyssey,” Christopher Nolan ventured into the realm of fantasy for the first time, realizing a time of towering monsters, swirling whirlpools, and apparent magic. The production is a true showcase for his longtime collaborator, production visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, who began working on the film‘s elaborate set pieces far ahead of production.

Industry observers note that “What’s essential is having the visual effects team be part of the main unit through prep, through the shoot, everything — and not treating you guys as somebody that’s going to come on afterwards and add to the film,” Nolan said, speaking with Jackson during a panel following a Visual Effects Society screening of “The Odyssey” at the IMAX auditorium of AMC Theatres’ Universal Cinema location in Los Angeles. The discussion was moderated by Guillermo del Toro. Related Stories ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés.

“What I’ve found through the years is to treat the effects as a remedial thing that is separate from everything is a big mistake,” del Toro added. “The beauty of it and the respect for the crafts is to integrate them early enough so that they are part of a physical solution as well as the post-production solution.”.

Sources indicate that the panel offered a detailed breakdown of several standout sequences in “The Odyssey,” including the early encounter with the Cyclops, which was realized with a mix of animatronic puppetry, digital effects, and a performance by clowning veteran Bill Irwin. Nolan shared that Jackson, who started as a model maker, is always one of his earliest collaborators — he was the first person to read the script for “Oppenheimer,” even. Integrating the various design elements of the Cyclops required a constant conversation from pre-production through the editing room.

“We were forced to shorten the time we had to build it,” Jackson began. Nolan then offered a joke: “I like the word forced. It’s good. I’m getting used to my crew members just vilifying me completely as we sit in these Q&As.”.

Sources indicate that “We both know that the result of being forced to trim away all the more complex parts of the plan resulted in a solution that was better than it would’ve been if we had continued with the original plan,” Jackson continued. “We basically just made a very, very simple marionette, which had still detailed solid components for the physical body, but just missed out on all the complicated joints and where the parts intersected. But the fact that it was simple and moved in a fascinating way that had a life of its own became really compelling.”.

“I knew that one day you’d be sitting here and Guillermo del Toro would say it was perfectly integrated, so it’s all worth it,” Nolan mentioned.

As with many industry Q&As these days, the topic of artificial intelligence’s impact on the filmmaking process, particularly on the field of visual effects, was addressed. Nolan, Jackson, and del Toro each emphasized the need for human oversight of the technology’s implementation, suggesting that “The Odyssey” could not have been realized without the conversations that happened across the film’s various departments.

“In an age with artificial intelligence looming — with synthetic creativity around us, or whatever — it’s actually very important to acknowledge the artistry that goes into the compositing process,” Nolan said. “My demand on the compositors and the animators is always to be using their eye rather than their brain, if you like, rather than simulating things or creating a simulation reality. I want them to look at it with an artist’s eye: the way matte painters who were working on glass paintings did, so that there’s an impressionistic quality in the composites.”.

In a recent development, “The defense of the human touch and the defense of the craft is as urgent, if not more urgent, to VFX because it is the one that has gotten assailed the fastest by things like AI, which was not invented or demanded from any artist,” del Toro mentioned. “It was demanded and created by people that were alien to that and appeal only to time and money mostly.”.

“Well, time and money and also a misunderstanding of the process,” Nolan said.

“You’re absolutely going to need artists to know even whether the upcoming tools have delivered things that you want. You need people to be able to assess that,” Jackson remarked.

Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let customers scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers.
  • Google says it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web.
  • Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let owners run scans free of cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let customers scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the company discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with fresh scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Google says it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a newly introduced service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let owners run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google released the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One users, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

You'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

It’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

Recent findings suggest that but perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that users want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the firm hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

In a recent development, there isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

Industry observers note that if your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Sources indicate that finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when you meet Mandy in Grand Theft Auto 6 for the first time, you can pick between the "defuse" and "provoke" dialogue options to determine how Jason is going to approach her during the conversation.
  • If you're curious about what is the best dialogue option to pick in this scene, we've got you covered.
  • When talking to Mandy, the game gives you the option to either provoke or defuse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when you meet Mandy in Grand Theft Auto 6 for the first time, you can pick between the "defuse" and "provoke" dialogue options to determine how Jason is going to approach her during the conversation. This encounter takes place during the "Pipework" quest in Chapter 1. Jason is doing some jobs for Brian, who asked him to collect the rent from a couple of tenants. Mandy is one of them, but her condition for paying the rent is that her sink be fixed, and she specifically asked for Jason to come and help her.

If you're curious about what is the best dialogue option to pick in this scene, we've got you covered. Here's a rundown on whether you should defuse or provoke Mandy in GTA 6.

When talking to Mandy, the game gives you the option to either provoke or defuse. Both options are valid, as they lead to the same outcome: Mandy locks herself in a room while telling Jason to leave. Although Mandy implies that she has feelings towards Jason, this encounter is not connected to the game's romance system. Jason will not have sex with Mandy, no matter which option you pick. However, depending on the dialogue option you pick, the scene will play out differently, letting you see distinct reactions from Mandy.

This whole situation happens after Jason fixes Mandy's sink and removes whatever was obstructing the pipe. She offers him some cigars as a reward for helping her. However, the conversation escalates as she asks Jason if he doesn't like her. She goes out of her house due to some confusion involving her neighbor and throws the cigars on the ground.

You can leave after that, as you have already completed the quest by this point, but you will miss the chance to talk to Mandy. Instead of leaving, return to Mandy's house to find her sitting in the living room (but don't forget to pick up the cigars from the ground). Press L2/LT and the "provoke" and "defuse" options will appear.

If you choose to calm her down, Mandy will ask Jason to stop his mind games, while telling him that they make him more attractive. On the other hand, if you decide to push her buttons, then she will basically threaten Jason. Regardless of which option you choose, eventually Mandy moves to her room and lock herself inside.

In a recent development, maybe that's for the best. Afterall, if you investigate outside of Mandy's house and the inside of her trunk, you may find some interesting items that point to Mandy being... well, unpredictable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iPhone Duo has been out for about 3 weeks now, and I’ve happily been using mine since launch day. Many people have made a big deal about the app situation, but I’d largely say most apps I rely on are updated for iOS 27.0 at least.

Recent findings suggest that that said, a fair number of apps are still from iOS 26 and earlier, and those apps have letterboxing. In my time since trying the phone, I feel one quick adjustment could make the letterboxing a lot less of an matter.

Right now, on the home screen, iPhone Duo allows you to long press an app and open it in Split View. All iPhone Duo apps allow Split View, even if the developer hasn’t compiled it for iOS 27 or 27.1.

In a recent development, one of the beautiful things about iPhone Duo Split View is the fact that you don’t have to decide what you’re splitting right away. On the other half of the display, you’ll see your home screen, and you can later decide what app to open.

It has been revealed that so, given the fact that a non iOS 27 app will only occupy around half of the inner display anyways, I feel like it’d make sense to have an option to open every non-optimized app in Split View by default – rather than needing to select it every time. Or, better yet, toggle certain apps to always open in Split View.

Certain apps, even if they’re optimized for iOS 27, don’t quite feel right spread across the wider inner display of iPhone Duo – so it’d be nice to always have them in a half split without needing to think about it.

This would be a small UX improvement that I feel would go a long way, so if Apple could implement this on iPhone Duo – it’d certainly help out the app situation. While they’re at it, it’d be nice to have Slide Over on the iPhone Duo, for when you want to quickly see a smaller app on top of your full screen app.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, you can't fairly judge a phone's true merits after a few hours, or even a few days.
  • In a recent development, is this one of the best foldable phones you can buy?
  • According to recent reports, the iPhone Duo is a first-generation product, and it offers a different proposition from the tried-and-tested formula of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you can't fairly judge a phone's true merits after a few hours, or even a few days. I’ve been using the iPhone Duo as my daily driver for the last fortnight, and now feel I’ve had time to take stock of what shines (and what doesn’t) when it comes to Apple’s first foldable phone.

In a recent development, is this one of the best foldable phones you can buy? Unquestionably. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t some imperfections to be wary of. The good news for anyone on the fence about this $2,000 handset is that even after 14 days, the wow factor hasn’t worn off. Folding away what's essentially an iPad mini and tucking it into your pocket just doesn’t get old — even though I wish more of the apps were optimized for the 1:4:1 aspect ratio displays.

According to recent reports, the iPhone Duo is a first-generation product, and it offers a different proposition from the tried-and-tested formula of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. But even when you compare the Duo to Samsung’s eighth iteration of a foldable phone, it’s impressive just how much Apple has got right.

In a recent development, speaking of the Galaxy Z Fold 8, I’ve seen a lot of reviewers — including my colleague Mark Spoonauer — wishing the Duo was closer to that phone’s 201g weight. When I first picked up the Duo at Apple HQ, I didn’t mind the 254g weight — and I still don’t. It’s concentrated when folded but balances out when the device is open. The iPhone Duo 2 will surely trim the fat a bit, but for me the extra heft isn’t a strike against the Duo yet.

Here are a few other things that I like best about the iPhone Duo.

It’s obvious, I know — but being able to run two apps simultaneously on my iPhone has proved a huge productivity win time and time again. For example, we cover a lot of live events at Tom’s Guide, and the iPhone Duo lets me keep Slack open on one panel with a livestream broadcast locked to the other.

It has been revealed that it also makes uploading images a cinch. Keep the Photos app open on the left with Google Drive on the right, and you can just drag and drop pictures into your desired location. It’s a huge time-saver that I’ve gotten very used to.

In a recent development, this Duo-exclusive feature hasn’t been getting as much appreciation as I’d have thought, considering we’re accelerating towards Thanksgiving and the holidays at an alarming rate. If, like me, you’ll be trying to get sugar-fueled children to sit still for Christmas photos, this camera trick will come in clutch.

Fire up the Duo’s camera and when the phone is unfolded the outer screen will play some clips of Snoopy to grab their attention while you snap the perfect portrait shot. The only downside I’ve noticed is that the kids won’t be looking exactly at the camera because the Duo’s 48MP Dual Fusion camera is positioned to the side. Still, it’s a pretty ingenious little feature that’ll earn its stripes on Thanksgiving weekend.

Recent findings suggest that every single workday for years, my phone has sat face up on the desk, occasionally illuminating with a notification or a call. Since I started using the iPhone Duo, I prop the little guy up in “Tent Mode”, where the outer display indicates my calendar, a photo slideshow or the music I’m listening to. If needed, you can also stream content on the outer display.

Sources indicate that for the most part, I use it to display multiple time zones at a glance. I’m based in London and routinely need to work with colleagues in Upcoming York and Los Angeles. It’s true you can achieve the same effect with a regular iPhone and a MagSafe stand, but if you’re hot desking or working from coffee shops, then being able to prop the iPhone Duo into StandBy mode all by itself is a significant win.

As I noted at the outset, not everything is perfect with this phone, and there are a couple of things that give me pause when I get asked if the Duo is worth the price of admission. I’ve already mentioned app incompatibility, so I won’t rehash that here, but here are the two substantial sticking points that I bump into again and again when using the iPhone as my daily driver.

Apple is reportedly actively working on Face ID for the iPhone Duo 2 (along with adding an Action Button) and it can’t come soon enough. I don’t have anything necessarily against Touch ID — except in this case because I’m left-handed. When I’m using my right hand, I can swipe up, thumb the power switch and unlock the Duo in a split second.

But the majority of the time, I instinctively pick up my phone with my left hand and curl my index finger around the back to hit the button that way. I’ve grown accustomed to it but it’s slower and more awkward than Face ID and feels like a step backwards in usability.

It has been revealed that the latest development beta includes something of a workaround: users will be able to activate the front-facing camera to unlock the phone within a 45-minute window of using their passcode or Touch ID. It's still in the early stages, but it could become a huge accessibility boost for lefties like myself.

Smaller tablets make for excellent notebook replacements, and this was one of the things I was most looking forward to using the iPhone Duo for. Alas, the only Apple Pencil I have in my possession is the Apple Pencil 2nd Generation from an aging iPad Pro. Which means I need to buy the Apple Pencil (USB-C) in order to use with my Duo.

I’ll admit, this is a minor hang-up; I expect many people already own the $75 Apple Pencil (USB-C) and are happy to have it working on the Duo. I’m just not one of them and would have appreciated if the $2,000 iPhone Duo worked with serviceable Apple tech I already own, rather than having to spend even more money to unlock its full potential.

Still, the good news is the Apple Pencil (USB-C) is at the moment reduced in the Black Friday sales, so if — like me — you haven’t picked up one to work with your Duo yet, now is the time to do so.

Though David Ellison has been around Hollywood for a while now, he’s undoubtedly our newest media mogul and still a fresh face when it comes to being the center stage headliner at fill-in-the-blank business media conference. There’s still a lot we don’t know about him and a lot of questions people have about his aims for Skydance, his politics, and his taste in movies.

So on Wednesday when he spoke with Andrew Ross Sorkin of the Fresh York Times at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday, he had a chance to get candid about a whole range of subjects. It’s early days at Skydance, with changes to the C-suite coming daily, so he’s still keeping his cards a little close to his sport jacket. But we did learn a few things about what he envisions for Skydance. Related Stories Christopher Nolan and Guillermo del Toro Break Down ‘The Odyssey’ Monsters and AI’s Limitations with Production VFX Supervisor Andrew Jackson ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Isn’t a Scene-Stealer — He’s Something Better.

“One of our guiding thematics has always been where entertainment is heading,” Ellison said. “It’s that great Gretsky quote, skate to where the puck is going, not to where the puck has been, and that’s been what’s guided the manufacturer.”.

Following a report that the world’s richest man had invested $1 billion into Ellison’s Skydance, leading many to think there’s some bigger picture brewing between Skydance and Starlink, Ellison did confirm that Musk is an investor and shareholder, and though he couldn’t comment on anything on which they may be collaborating, he’s welcoming the opportunity.

“He’s the greatest entrepreneur of all time,” Ellison noted. “He doesn’t invest in a lot of companies, so to have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege, and if there’s ever an opportunity to collaborate in the future, from our perspective it would be a privilege.”.

Sorkin did double back and ask if Ellison will still allow Alex Gibney’s “Musk” documentary to air on HBO as been planned. He said that HBO has a Pay-1 deal with A24, so of course they would honor that agreement, and they “believe in independence and we don’t believe in censorship of any kind.”.

One problem: A24 didn’t produce “Musk” as Ellison remarked. It’s a Bleecker Street film. So we’ll put a little asterisk on that answer.

Sources indicate that tom Cruise’s mega flop “Digger” has the ironic and unfortunate distinction of being the final movie released by Warner Bros. Discovery. And Ellison was asked “how risky” he would continue to be in the context of how much money “Digger” stands to lose. Ellison started by saying that Cruise is “one of the seminal artists of our time,” that Skydance has made eight movies previously with him, and they’re making a “Days of Thunder” sequel before (hopefully) heading into making “Top Gun 3.”.

Ellison then described a long story that involved sleeping on Hans Zimmer’s couch before landing on the age old, “what’s the budget?”.

“I spent the last 16 years of my life on the filmmaking side of this business. I have lived on set, I have slept on Hans Zimmer’s couch, I have been in editorial rooms for 20 hours non-stop, I do understand the creative process of this business,” Ellison stated. “The goal has to be in any film that you make is how do you reach the broadest possible audience for that particular story? There is no one size fits all approach. We will make franchise movies, we will make original stories, we will make genre pictures, we will tell stories aimed at audiences from every single walk of life. What is notable is that you size the budget to the potential addressable audience.”.

Sources indicate that sorkin pushed Ellison hard about what his politics are and who he voted for in the most recent election. He still did not get an answer, but he would not let slide some of the reports that President Trump himself asked about Paramount requesting that the studio make “Rush Hour 4.”.

“We are working with Brett [Ratner] on ‘Rush Hour 4,’ which is a sequel to an incredibly successful franchise,” Ellison confirmed. However, he noted the first time he heard about the prospect of that movie was when film chief Josh Goldstine walked into his office and mentioned it, not that it came from Trump, and that “there’s a lot of made up stories” out there.

Sources indicate that “Rush Hour” director Ratner as a reminder was in 2017 accused of sexual harassment and misconduct by six women as part of a Los Angeles Times report, including actresses Olivia Munn and Natasha Henstridge, claims that he denied. His most recent project was this year’s “Melania” documentary that was released by Amazon MGM.

One thing Ellison has been working with President Trump on is his desire to get passed a federal tax rebate for film productions in the U.S., and he told Sorkin his goal is to see the rebate passed by the end of this year, at which point the newly introduced Congress comes into office and a bill has to be reintroduced. He stated he had three meetings with the late Senator Lindsay Graham about the problems of film production leaving the country.

Ellison was staunch in pushing back on some data from the Tax Policy Center as shared by Sorkin that while subsidies do influence where productions choose to shoot, it’s not the same as creating measurable economic growth and that it just pulls workers away from other jobs and tourism.

In a recent development, “Categorically that’s just not true. When you actually look at the rebate in the United Kingdom, it has been a boom to their economy, same is true in Canada, same is true in Australia. All those other countries have those rebates because it pencils out,” Ellison noted. “If you look at Texas, Paramount was a part of building a 31 percent rebate for all of Taylor Sheridan’s productions. We had a meeting down there with the deputy governor that said, based on their own independent audit, for every dollar that was invested by the state returned $4.70.”.

He also stressed that it’s a misnomer that Tom Cruise is the one getting a tax break but that really it goes to helping union, working class film professionals who benefit.

“You are creating jobs, you are helping small businesses, and every other country that has done this in the past has done this because it is economically sustainable,” he added.

Ellison on numerous occasions in earnings calls and in other appearances has expressed his fondness for artificial intelligence and how he feels it’s going to transform Hollywood. He elaborated on that view a little more on Wednesday, calling it not just a tool for artists but a “creative unlock.”.

“Going back to the days of Pixar, the lesson was always be wrong as fast as possible…we’re going to be living in a world where you can make the movie not 10 times but 20 times before it gets put out,” Ellison mentioned. “We’re also living in a world where a $750K movie made $500 million because the cost of production has boxed out new voices.”.

He’s referring to “Obsession” there, but he also gave the example of the original “Terminator,” which Ellison stated James Cameron made for $4 million but today would cost $70 million. He felt the AI tools would help people to make those original stories, and he’s fully on board.

“The relationship we basically have with talent, our understanding of technology and how those two things are fused together, it’s a feedback loop,” Ellison remarked. “It is the art challenges the technology, technology inspires the art feedback loop. That is what is necessary to meet this moment in time and build the entertainment organization of the future.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Industry observers note that google released Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

In a recent development, to me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is right now open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Sources indicate that pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

According to recent reports, ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

Sources indicate that if you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A growing number of people are asking AI chatbots about their health issues, raising two major concerns: safety and privacy. Apple is now offering a safer way to do this through an Apple Health AI Usage Study.

This is actually one of Apple’s research studies, but those volunteering to take part in it will be able to ask health questions – with three key assurances not guaranteed by other AI chatbots ….

In a recent development, apple launched its Research app back in 2019 with the goal of allowing customers to help universities and medical institutions with health studies. You typically agree to share certain anonymized information from the Apple Health app in order to provide data that can advance medical research. You may also be asked to complete questionnaires.

The Apple Health AI Usage Study is one of these, but it works in a somewhat different way. You’ll still be invited to share some of your health data, but will also be able to ask an AI system questions about your health.

When you ask health questions of a typical AI chatbot, you don’t know how reliable those answers may be or what will happen to your data. Apple study offers three assurances:.

Apple says that answers will be generated by the same platform used by healthcare professionals.

The study is conducted in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a leading clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals that generates answers using medical information from established sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature.

The answers provided to you will include links to peer-reviewed clinical citations.

As you’d expect from Apple, there are strong privacy protections, including the assurance that your data will not be used to train AI models.

According to recent reports, the study is designed from the ground up with privacy protections, transparency, and clinical guardrails, and study data will not be used to train AI models. Participants retain control over whether to share any HealthKit metrics or survey responses, and Apple has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information.

CNET reports on Apple’s assurance that none of your chats will be retained.

It has been revealed that openEvidence will delete both question and response data within 24 hours. A small group of Apple researchers will have access to coded versions of survey responses, separated from personally identifiable information, summaries of conversations and categories of the most common conversation types.

Access to the study is presently limited to owners in the US by downloading the app. If you try it, please do share your thoughts in the comments.

They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

It has been revealed that bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very promptly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time Fresh York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

  • A leaker today says that the iPhone 20 Pro is getting a latest and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera, but details are unclear ….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the biggest improvement to iPhone photo quality that Apple could make would be to give the device a larger sensor. There have been two reports suggesting this is on the way, although with a potentially rather large catch.

A leaker today says that the iPhone 20 Pro is getting a latest and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera, but details are unclear ….

There are two main reasons people still buy standalone cameras despite having an iPhone in their pocket wherever they go. The first is lens quality: iPhones have small plastic lenses compared to the far larger and more sophisticated glass lenses used with dedicated cameras.

The second is sensor size. All other things being equal, a larger sensor will capture more light and provide a higher quality image. Current smartphone sensors are absolutely tiny compared to those used in even mid-range consumer cameras.

We’ve seen two previous reports suggesting that a larger sensor is on the way for future iPhones. One of these suggested that it would be coming in 2027 or 2028, although a later one suggested the latter date was more likely.

The reports were not without a catch, however, suggesting that the larger sensor would only be for the telephoto lens and would have a 200MP resolution. Squeezing more pixels into a given sensor size tends to sacrifice low light capabilities in return for higher resolution. This is less likely to be an problem with a telephoto lens, which is normally used outdoors rather than inside.

What I’d really love to see is a significantly larger sensor for the main camera, with no increase in resolution. This would improve low light performance and overall image quality.

A brief report from leaker Ice Universe suggests that the iPhone 20 Pro will get a new and more sophisticated sensor for the main camera.

iPhone 20 Pro to feature a newly introduced sensor using 17nm logic process for its main camera next year.

There are no further details, so we don’t know whether the size of the sensor will be increased or remain the same.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week saw a truly epic outage to Microsoft 365, with a huge number of consumers unable to send and receive emails.
  • Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected ….
  • It has been revealed that the tech giant noted at the time that it was a technical issue and not a cyber attack, and that it was working hard to fix the problem, admitting that it was taking longer than expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week saw a truly epic outage to Microsoft 365, with a huge number of consumers unable to send and receive emails. The tech giant has now admitted that at the worst point, more than 80% of its servers were unresponsive.

Microsoft has now explained what went wrong, stating that the mistake that led to the failure was actually made all the way back in July without being detected ….

It has been revealed that the tech giant noted at the time that it was a technical issue and not a cyber attack, and that it was working hard to fix the problem, admitting that it was taking longer than expected. Microsoft also denied that it was related to the thousands of layoffs unveiled the previous month.

People were understandably unimpressed at the scale of the outage and the time taken to fix it, although meme creators were having fun.

Recent findings suggest that sorry but you have to be change the name now. Thems the rules pic.twitter.com/5UttZ8nt9f.

It certainly points out that when you base your business on cloud services, you also take the risk that comes with that.

Platform head Charles Lamanna admitted the severity of the problem.

It has been revealed that in less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

He mentioned it resulted from a combination of two concerns. The firm maintains two independent network gateway systems, one of which failed, meaning that the remaining gateway took the full load. That wouldn’t have been a problem on its own, Microsoft stating that each one has enough capacity to handle all traffic. However, a mistake made back in July led to a cascading failure.

Recent findings suggest that A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. This was due to lock contention inside an internal process which caused the machine to become unavailable. This defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers […].

Recent findings suggest that the initial change in behavior first started deployment in July of this year. The enhancement went through safe deployment and saturated globally over several weeks, during which time no problems were observed. For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact. Our normal load testing did not detect the latent glitch because the different traffic and SKU mix used in our test labs. The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on our weaker hardware SKUs with fewer cores.

In other words, the update wasn’t tested under the conditions in which it was most likely to fail.

In a recent development, while the manufacturer claims that the incident is unrelated to laying off staff and replacing them with AI systems, I find myself extremely skeptical. It seems inconceivable that a company of Microsoft’s size could make what appears to be a schoolboy error of this magnitude unless there were insufficient engineers working on the patch. Please share your own thoughts in the comments.

#39541. Where Are the Women? Zero Female Directors on Blumhouse Atomic’s Theatrical Slate for 2027

Where Are the Women? Zero Female Directors on Blumhouse Atomic’s Theatrical Slate for 2027

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that blumhouse Atomic put a number on just about everything at its “Business of Fear” press conference on Wednesday.
  • Sources indicate that it has 10 movies scheduled to open nationwide in 2027.
  • “So we are working with a lot of women,” Blum remarked after running through several names.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that blumhouse Atomic put a number on just about everything at its “Business of Fear” press conference on Wednesday. The merged and renamed horror studio put its share of this year’s worldwide horror box office at more than 50 percent.

Sources indicate that it has 10 movies scheduled to open nationwide in 2027. Six are originals. Four are upcoming franchise entries. Seven come from “emerging voices,” including three first-time feature filmmakers. At the end of the day’s first panel, IndieWire asked Jason Blum about a number that didn’t make the slides: How many of those 10 movies were directed by women? Zero.

“So we are working with a lot of women,” Blum remarked after running through several names. “They didn’t fall in next year’s slate.” The Blumhouse founder and CEO added that it was “very, very notable to make sure that the directors reflect our audience and look like our audience, so we’re always making a big effort to make sure that that happens.” Related Stories ‘Bedford Park’ Trailer: Sundance Winner Stars Moon Choi, Who Falls for the Other Driver in Her Mother’s Car Accident David Ellison on Elon Musk’s Skydance Investment, Trump and ‘Rush Hour 4,’ and Whether He Would’ve Made ‘Digger’.

It was the last question, and neither Atomic Monster founder James Wan nor Blumhouse president Abhijay Prakash expanded on Blum’s answer. Blumhouse Television president Melissa Aouate then took the microphone to moderate the second conversation.

She was the only woman onstage across both discussions, and though Blum had just cited “Scarpetta” showrunner Liz Sarnoff in his answer to IndieWire, Aouate went on to interview four men, including another company president, about their work while no one asked about hers.

In a later statement to IndieWire, Aouate mentioned she welcomed the chance to bring television into a conversation largely about film and wanted to find “more connective tissue between our film and television slates.”.

“By most measures, opportunities for women have contracted in so many areas of the industry, and we take that very seriously,” she said, citing Sarnoff on “Scarpetta,” Cynthia Childs on the “Worst Ever” franchise, and Emma Tammi on “Five Nights at Freddy’s” as examples of major women storytellers working at the company.

Recent findings suggest that “The industry still has a long way to go, and so do we,” she noted. “That’s work we take seriously, and we’re all working to see our slate reflect it.”.

In a recent development, A Blumhouse Atomic spokesperson told IndieWire that women directed 25 percent of the organization’s 2026 film slate. The spokesperson did not specify which titles or release formats counted toward that figure, but both 2026 films Blum cited onstage at least premiered at home.

Recent findings suggest that “We had ‘The Last Kiss’ by a female director,” Blum said of Yoko Okumura, whose film debuted in September, shortly after Kate Dolan’s “SOULM8TE” went straight to digital in August. Blum nodded to that project, too, and he also mentioned Tammi, who got a nationwide theatrical release for “Five Nights at Freddy’s” in 2023 before getting hired back for its 2025 sequel.

By the manufacturer’s own accounting, that second gig made obvious financial sense.

Recent findings suggest that prakash plainly explained on Wednesday that when Blumhouse Atomic calculates a return on investment, it divides worldwide ticket sales by the production budget. The first “Freddy’s” earned nearly $300 million worldwide on a reported $20 million budget, while 2025’s “Five Nights at Freddy’s 2” brought in another $240 million against a $51 million budget. By Prakash’s formula, the two films grossed roughly 7.6 times their combined costs.

IndieWire counted 27 features from Blumhouse and Atomic Monster that played in at least 600 U.S. theaters from 2021 through 2025. Our review counted co-productions once and included the first “Five Nights at Freddy’s,” which debuted simultaneously on Peacock.

Still, women helmed only two, and Tammi directed both. (Asked whether she would return for a third “Freddy’s” film, a Blumhouse Atomic spokesperson told IndieWire, “No updates to share on the next installment of ‘Five Nights at Freddy’s’ at this time.”).

According to recent reports, looking back to streaming, there’s a meaningful difference in opportunity for women. Over the same five years, 22 features from Blumhouse and the former Atomic Monster debuted in the U.S. via streaming, premium TV, or digital on demand without a theatrical run. Women directed or co-directed nine of those projects, accounting for roughly 41 percent of films. That’s compared with 7 percent of the companies’ nationwide theatrical releases.

“Obsession” and “Backrooms,” of course, came up repeatedly. Curry Barker’s indie topped the firm’s horror chart with more than $500 million worldwide. Kane Parsons’ feature adaptation of his YouTube series earned another $400 million. “Indie horror is suddenly performing as well or better than studio horror,” Blum said. A decade ago, he estimated, those same movies “would’ve made $25 million at the box office.”.

He further credited Barker’s years on YouTube with teaching him how to read an audience, noting he’s producing Barker’s second feature, “Anything but Ghosts,” due out next May. Wan also remembered an early Zoom with Parsons, who was young enough that his dad was on the call then.

Recent findings suggest that by the time IndieWire asked where women fit into the 2027 slate, Blum and Wan had thoroughly detailed what they saw in these two young men and how they helped each grow. On the second panel, Aouate asked Atomic Monster president Michael Clear what it takes for a fresh director to get his attention. He described what he tells agents about someone who hasn’t directed a horror scene.

Sources indicate that “It doesn’t mean I might not work with them in the future, but have them go direct a scare in their apartment at two minutes. That’s what we want,” he said. Of Parsons’ “Backrooms” short, he recalled, “It scared me, and that was it.”.

Sources indicate that the organization didn’t say how often shorts directed by women reach decision-makers like Clear. But asked how Blumhouse Atomic seeks out women directors these days, a spokesperson cited “traditional channels and less obvious ones, like our Screamwriting Lab and the horror shorts and online talent our team scouts.”.

Industry observers note that one woman whose work has caught their attention online is Heidi Wong, who built a following of millions telling illustrated horror stories on TikTok. Last month at New York Comic Con, Wong and Blum announced a deal to develop short films together. Her social media success seems to make her exactly the kind of emerging talent Blumhouse Atomic wants to cultivate. Whether that partnership leads to a theatrical feature remains to be seen.

Eight years ago, Blum apologized after telling Polygon that fewer women were inclined to direct horror movies. In response, researcher Stephen Follows examined three decades of feature films released in U.S. theaters, from 1988 through 2017. Women accounted for just 5.9 percent of horror directors in his sample. Importantly, that figure tells us who got a film into theaters. It notes very little about who wanted to make one or how close they came.

Of course, the disparity extends beyond horror. Across all genres last year, women accounted for 13 percent of directors among the 250 highest-grossing films at the domestic box office. That’s down from 16 percent in 2024, per San Diego State University’s Celluloid Ceiling report.

Blumhouse Atomic also has six distribution partners on its 2027 slate. Plus, films that ultimately premiere at home may have been developed with theaters in mind. The same organization spokesperson emphasized to IndieWire that women on the company’s creative team often find and develop major movies, too, running some of the brand’s most beloved franchises.

Industry observers note that over the five years IndieWire examined, though, Tammi was still the only woman to direct a Blumhouse movie that reached horror audiences in theaters nationwide. Yes, those 10 release dates for next year could be an accident of timing, with real gender parity just around the corner. But years of women getting fewer chances to scare audiences on the significant screen suggest something more enduring than a scheduling coincidence. For a business built on knowing what scares people, Hollywood’s horror industry seems remarkably unafraid of shutting women out.

Tech Report: You Can Try WhatsApp's Newly introduced Disappearing Text Messages Early

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (444 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices.
  • As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too.
  • As WABetaInfo highlights, the first time you use this feature, WhatsApp will present a pop-up explaining the feature, how "View Once text gives you more privacy," and that when you send the message, it'll disappear from the chat after the recipient opens it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As WABetaInfo highlights, the first time you use this feature, WhatsApp will present a pop-up explaining the feature, how "View Once text gives you more privacy," and that when you send the message, it'll disappear from the chat after the recipient opens it. WhatsApp also explains that recipients cannot share, forward, save, or take screenshots of View Once text messages. Recipients won't see the text appear in the usual chat interface, either; instead, your recipient will need to open the message in a separate window. Once they close this page, the message disappears.

Recent findings suggest that as mentioned above, this feature is right now in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That stated, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.).

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest upgrade. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

NCIS has enjoyed a resurgent year on CBS, and part of that has to do with the return of Sam Hanna as a regular presence on Tuesday nights. The former NCIS: Los Angeles Senior Special Agent and partner of Grisha Callen (Chris O'Donnell), played memorably by LL COOL J, finally has his own show again after NCIS: New York came together quickly earlier this year. So far, the results speak for themselves, too. The latest procedural spin-off debuted to a strong 5.62 million average viewers earlier this fall, trailing only the flagship series as the most-watched show on Tuesday night that week, and it has since held steady with an average of 5.18 million viewers over the first three episodes. As part of a three-show night, the franchise's visit to the Significant Apple is fitting right in.

Industry observers note that with just two episodes left to go until the holiday break, Sam has reestablished himself well in his hometown. Latest York brings him back to the titular city after years of special operations on a personal mission to investigate the death of a friend and Navy reservist, only to link up with the local NCIS team and fit right in with the crew. Rolling with a new partner in the roguish Nick Schaeffer (Scott Caan) under the leadership of Assistant Special Agent-in-Charge Robyn Wells (Jennifer Beals), he's been busy solving crimes throughout familiar streets and neighborhoods involving everyone from corrupt politicians to jewelry store thieves. Next year, when the series returns, though, he'll be taking naval crime investigation to a new night for a special occasion.

It has been revealed that CBS unveiled its midseason premiere dates earlier this week and, with it, confirmed that NCIS: New York would be getting a special Sunday night broadcast at the end of January. Right after the network hosts the AFC Championship Game, a new episode will debut, giving Sam and the team a massive lead-in for one night only. Otherwise, episodes will continue to air in the normal 9 p.m. ET/PT time slot on Tuesdays. After wrapping up for the fall on December 8, the entire NCIS slate is slated to pick back up starting on January 12.

Industry observers note that along with the rest of the NCIS slate, Latest York is also about to go on break to celebrate Thanksgiving. Next week, no new episodes of the procedural franchise will air, with programming returning as usual on December 1. When it does return, viewers will be treated to "The River," which revolves around the disappearance of a Marine sergeant in New Jersey. The team will be called in to investigate why he suddenly vanished, though it may have something to do with his decision to flee Quantico the night before a high-stakes mission. Expect the whole team to get involved, including Addy Ross (Jacqueline Byers), Wyatt Sellers (Shane Harper), and Sean Sullivan (Devin Druid).

NCIS: New York airs Tuesday nights on CBS at 9 p.m. and will air its special Sunday night broadcast after the AFC Championship on January 31. Stay tuned here at Collider for more updates on the future of the latest NCIS spin-off.

#39533. ‘The Altruists’ Review: Netflix’s Slight Sam Bankman-Fried Series Tells a Strange, Crooked Love Story

‘The Altruists’ Review: Netflix’s Slight Sam Bankman-Fried Series Tells a Strange, Crooked Love Story

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Netflix’s “The Altruists,” the latest limited series about a modern-day tech scandal, posits a few sound-enough theories about what drives its featured fraudster to steal $8 billion of customers’ money.
  • Arrested development and severe personalities are part and parcel for any tech founder story, so much so that, as a bleak sign of the times, they’re already being parodied.
  • Such echoes lend “The Altruists” a sense of “been there, broke that” amid a crowded Founders Fall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix’s “The Altruists,” the latest limited series about a modern-day tech scandal, posits a few sound-enough theories about what drives its featured fraudster to steal $8 billion of customers’ money. For instance, Sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle) grows up playing games but never actually grows up, so he struggles to perceive his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, as anything beyond a game he’s meant to win. The unkempt, dead-eyed co-founder similarly has a hard time distinguishing between theoretical and actual consequences, so when a “mathematically optimal” strategy doesn’t pay out, all he sees is a smaller-than-expected number on the balance sheet — not a retirement account squandered or a college education lost. Related Stories Skydance to Combine Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios as One Massive Studio ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés.

Arrested development and severe personalities are part and parcel for any tech founder story, so much so that, as a bleak sign of the times, they’re already being parodied. (In “The Audacity,” Billy Magnussen’s insecure, second-rate CEO loses his shit when a psych test shows he’s not on the spectrum.) On top of these familiar traits, “The Altruists” adds familiar language in the form of ear-piercing dog whistles — Sam speaks of of “moving fast” and “breaking things” one too many times — which make clear our antihero belongs among the villainous Silicon Valley set. He’s as much a product of the times as a very “special” boy.

Such echoes lend “The Altruists” a sense of “been there, broke that” amid a crowded Founders Fall. (Even if “The Social Reckoning” wasn’t for you, we all just rewatched “The Dropout,” no?) But creator and co-showrunner Graham Moore, alongside co-showrunner and executive producer Jacqueline Hoyt, center their scammer’s analysis around a fresh(ish) yet timeless vantage point: Sam is in love with Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), and he has no idea how to express it. Their doomed romance sparks the creation and destruction of the third-largest digital currency exchange in the world (plus, you know, the subsequent prison sentences), as their inability to make sense of their emotions sullies their ethical ambitions for making billions (which were already pretty muddy).

It’s a shame, then, that their relationship proves as shallow as it is annoying. Wrapped in interminable, indicative nerd quirks — stutters and stammers, over-explanations and misplaced pride, regular references to Harry Potter, LARP, and math camp — Sam and Caroline’s grand romance isn’t sustainable enough entertainment to support an eight-hour story, nor is it explored with enough sincerity to break your heart (or expand your mind). Boyle and Garner’s performances are committed and their transformations convincing, but they’re in service of one theory about two people’s core deficiency that isn’t as revealing or rewarding as it needs to be.

Sam and Caroline’s meet-cute takes place — where else — at work. In 2016, Sam is an ambitious go-getter on Wall Street. His custom algorithms have earned attention from the higher-ups after successfully predicting the election results and then trading off those results to the tune of $150 million in profit. …but then those same algorithms doubled down and ended up losing twice what they initially made. So, as punishment, Sam is sent to interview interns, where he meets and bonds with a fellow trader.

During an introductory quiz, Caroline determines there’s no prize for second place, which means it’s the same as last place, so the “mathematically optimal strategy is to go all-in every time.” It’s the same strategy Sam used to win when he was an intern, and although Caroline goes bust, she’s hits significant with Sam. His parents taught at Stanford, so he went to MIT to get away from them. Her parents taught at MIT, so she went to Stanford. They both were expected to be child math prodigies, but neither “prodigied.” Her ultimate goal is to solve the global water crisis. His is goal is equally altruistic, if much more vague.

“Look, I know I haven’t done it yet,” Sam says to Caroline. “Little things here and there, sure, but the significant thing? I’m a little behind schedule. But I’m going to do it.”.

His conviction wins her over — especially when they meet again, by chance, at a meeting for Effective Altruists — and soon enough they’re misreading flirtations and fumbling through his first sexual encounter. As they leave Wall Street behind to focus on “the major thing,” “The Altruists” jumps ahead to its second predominant timeline: Where their initial courtship and company start-ups take place in “Part 1: Rise,” even more screentime is dedicated to “Part II: Fall,” which picks up in 2022 when evidence of their theft starts to leak amid a massive party in the Bahamas.

In a recent development, the multiple-timeline structure ostensibly juxtaposes past promises from present betrayals, but it’s hardly necessary to get the point across (“how things have changed” doesn’t hit as hard when the characters look the same) and actively harmful to the supporting cast. Using “Rise” as the A-plot and “Fall” as the B-plot keeps Sam and Caroline in the center of things, which proves exhausting when they keep repeating themselves and strands everyone else in one-note (or sometimes no-note) archetypes who mainly exist to yell at the two leads.

In a recent development, sam Trabucco (Alex Lawther) is the mirror version of Sam Bankman-Fried, a sweet, self-assured kid who actually believes in what FTX is doing, until the hard truth of what they’ve actually done sends him fleeing to the open seas. (SBF stays put, living in his delusion of innocence.) Nishad Singh (Karan Soni) is another mirror, first as a friend from the neighborhood who bonded with Mr. Bankman (Paul Reiser) and Mrs. Fried (Robin Weigert) in a way Sam never could, and later as a fellow sufferer of unrequited love for a co-worker, only his heart is pure where Sam’s is tainted.

Eight hours of the immoral, motormouthed, future-then-former billionaire is a lot to tolerate, especially when his greatest obstacle is one we know he’ll never overcome: Sam and Caroline may be stupidly brilliant with numbers, but they’re just plain stupid when it comes to emotions. “I don’t think you can smart your way out of feelings,” Sam is told when our central couple first starts dating — but that doesn’t stop them from trying. Start to finish, Sam never says the words, “I love you,” despite each episode pivoting around a noxious will-they-or-won’t-they relationship that ebbs and flows between a full-on, loud-and-proud romance and a business partnership manufactured to keep them together when logic alone could not.

Tolerance may vary, but after a few hours, “The Altruists” is too cutesy, too aware of its own cuteness, and ultimately too dedicated to the wrong questions: What went wrong with FTX has been explained again and again, and the series doesn’t pass up its chance to play the hits. (It’s “inspired by” a series of Upcoming York Magazine articles.) But “The Altruists” has the chance to consider what went wrong with Sam and Caroline’s souls, and it doesn’t dig deep enough to expose anything more than emptiness.

At its best, “The Altruists” is a whirlwind depiction of love not as a beautiful, life-saving devotion, but as an illogical and immoral excuse to wreak havoc. (Think of it as the most unlikely spinoff to “The Last of Us.”) Sam and Caroline use each other to justify unscrupulous (and illegal) actions that stack up until they’re trapped by the sheer scope of their misjudgment. But at least they’re trapped together. It’s a love story and an anti-love story at once; the audience sees the latter and the subjects convince themselves it’s the former.

That’s fascinating territory to explore, thematically and internally, but Moore and Hoyt’s series tells you what it’s about — explicitly, repeatedly, unmistakably — and then reiterates that statement over and over as the situations escalate. Ultimately, it gets caught in the same quandary as its subjects: The relationship’s pointed lack of evolution proves more redundant than revelatory, so when it comes to emotional enlightenment, “The Altruists” is out of its depth.

“The Altruists” premieres Thursday, November 19 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, GTA 6, like many other Grand Theft Auto games before it, offers several missions with a choice. Generally, it's "should you kill or spare someone," but that choice alone can feel huge in that moment. I can't tell you how many times I've known people who have paused the action and looked up the consequences of a choice.

Recent findings suggest that that said, in GTA 6, not every choice is as heavy as it seems. Here's what you should do about Arnold, and whether you should kill or spare him early in the game, when you're just getting your bearings as Jason in the Florida Keys.

Early on in GTA 6, you'll meet Brian, the character who's essentially your first crime boss. Brian runs a marina out in the Florida Keys, getting up to all sorts of debauchery facilitated through his vehicles and associates. As Jason starts to become more and more entwined with Brian's interests, he'll start asking him to do bigger and bigger jobs.

One of those jobs deals with Brian's old friend Arnold. Brian and Arnold have had a working relationship for many years, but now that Arnold has stopped answering Brian's calls, it's clear something is going on. Brian asks him to investigate the issue on-site, leading to a confrontation with Arnold and his crew.

Recent findings suggest that A car chase ensues, and Jason is quickly pulled into an out-of-control situation, chasing Arnold across dangerous bridges and into a neighborhood. Depending on how the chase goes, Arnold generally gets out of his car and starts running on foot, and Brian gives him the go-ahead to "take care of him.".

Recent findings suggest that here's where the choice comes in. You can either let Arnold get away, or take him out from afar and end the mission right there.

Sources indicate that killing him will result in a "hardened" boost to your criminal meter, which can be good if you're trying to roleplay that type of Jason, or bad if you're not. Either way, it's functionally negligible, so if you prefer to handle the mission this way, this is one of the fastest methods. Once Arnold is taken out, you'll head back to meet up with another associate of Brian's, who will herald in a new deep-sea-diving mission type.

According to recent reports, letting him get away will have no negative impact on the storyline, and you won't "ruin" your relationship with Brian. In fact, Arnold will make an appearance later on, so you can get a better sense of what kind of character he is, rather than taking Brian's word at face value based on the 30 seconds you see him. In any case, it's OK to make either choice, and you won't need to reload a save or anything like that.

These kinds of choices are generally framed as substantial gravity-shifting alterations to the story of GTA 6, but that's not often the case. Don't stress too much about making decisions regarding minor characters, because the focus really is on Jason and Lucia. Their relationship and their individual hardened criminal profiles are the factors that will influence the dialogue and the story the most as you progress.
