Due to release in 2027, the independently produced short from Imoria Pictures runs about 15 minutes and centers on Littlefoot’s bond with his mother. You can check out the trailer and prepare for the heartbreak all over again below.

It has been revealed that four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

Sources indicate that you belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

It has been revealed that you belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

It has been revealed that you belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

According to recent reports, summer-Joules Saunders voices Littlefoot opposite Larissa Loeffler as his mother. Among the other young dinosaurs is a voice X-Men ’97 fans know as Gambit. A.J. LoCascio plays Petrie, the one member of the group who ought to be able to scout the road ahead if he could just work up the nerve to fly. Sarah Natochenny, who spent years voicing Ash Ketchum on Pokémon, plays Ducky, while Cristina Vee takes on Cera. Mark Meer, familiar to Mass Effect players as Commander Shepard, gets to be the adult laying down the law as Cera’s dad. Lever saved himself a part, too, as he has stepped into the role of Spike.

Industry observers note that lever first tried to get Littlefoot going in 2017, barely a year after Universal’s last sequel. In his anniversary post, he credited three years of work by artists, animators, musicians, and actors around the world who volunteered their time. The choice of what to do with those 15 minutes claims quite a bit about what stuck with them. Littlefoot’s mother only gets part of one movie with her son. Every kid who followed him through another 13 knows who taught him to look for the Great Valley in the first place.

Littlefoot is expected to release in 2027.

Latest Update: macOS 27.3 includes upcoming privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last month, Apple announced its intends to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents.
  • With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.
  • In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last month, Apple announced its intends to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access amid the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents.

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple indicates that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”.

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:.

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let consumers know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Industry observers note that crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Recent findings suggest that people can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

macOS 27.3 now warns you before giving an app full disk accessThat warning prompt is pretty scary! pic.twitter.com/J2qCKVWJRx.

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to enhancement their apps to account for situations where owners grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Sources indicate that finally, Apple indicates developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for upcoming installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

iOS 27.3 adds newly introduced face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo customers.
  • Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.
  • You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo customers. Most notably, it adds a fresh face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

In the Settings app, Apple notes:.

Industry observers note that use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

This isn’t Face ID. This new option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

According to recent reports, because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

Recent findings suggest that this face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this latest feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo users (myself included) have said Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1560 w)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

5 reasons why you should buy an older phone for Black Friday — and the best deals right now

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you're looking for a fresh phone this Black Friday, you may be inclined to pick the latest models.
  • Industry observers note that the real truth is that you're not going to miss out on much when you buy last year's flagship, or even a flagship from the year before.
  • Recent findings suggest that don't believe me?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you're looking for a fresh phone this Black Friday, you may be inclined to pick the latest models. They're newer, after all, and have the latest hardware and software that phone companies offer. But what if I told you that picking up an older phone might be a better option — especially if you're not looking to spend a lot of money?

Industry observers note that the real truth is that you're not going to miss out on much when you buy last year's flagship, or even a flagship from the year before. In fact, you might even end up with a device better than some of the best cheap phones that are at the moment on sale — for the simple reason that these are flagships that haven't been compromised by price.

Recent findings suggest that don't believe me? Here are five reasons why buying older phones is the better option during the Black Friday sales.

If you look at the cost of the latest flagship phones, you'll notice one thing they all have in common: they're expensive. Even if you do manage to get hold of those phones with some kind of discount, you're still going to be paying several hundred dollars — if not more. Older phones don't really have that concern.

Industry observers note that the thing about phones is that releasing a latest model doesn't magically make the previous generation disappear. Carriers and retailers lower the price to try and sell off inventory and during Black Friday that strategy gets turned up to 11.

For example, at the time of writing buying the Motorola Razr 2026 at Best Buy will cost you $799 — the full retail price. But last year's Motorola Razr 2025 is $250 less at $549. Likewise, Amazon is selling the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7 for $1,299, whereas the Z Fold 8 Ultra is presently $1,749.

If you've looked at a upcoming phone and thought "how is this any different from the last one?," you're not alone. Plenty of criticism has been leveled at phone companies for seemingly doing the bare minimum with each new generation, and customers realized that pretty quickly. So if the old one is basically the same as the new one, why does it matter which one you buy?

Take a look at the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, for example. It looks and feels almost identical to the Galaxy S25 Ultra. The chipset is newer, there's a Privacy Display feature, and charging speed has been increased — with 60W wired and 25W wireless charging compared to 45W and 15W on the S25 Ultra. Everything else is pretty much the same.

At the time of writing, the Galaxy S25 Ultra can be purchased for $859, though it has gone as low as $729 in the past. Meanwhile, an unlocked Galaxy S26 Ultra with no carrier obligations is on sale for $971. If you don't care about the few changes that have been made, then you can spend that extra money on something more important. Those savings could go toward some upcoming accessories, or just your usual monthly expenses.

In a recent development, A latest chipset could make major differences to how a phone performs. That's true to an extent, but it's not as though we're seeing gargantuan leaps in performance every single year.

Using the Galaxy S26 Ultra and S25 Ultra as an example again, you can see that the switch from a Snapdragon 8 Elite to the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 is noticeable. Benchmarking results show a rise in computing performance, especially in multi-core testing. The same is true for graphics performance, with an increase to the raw performance score and the average framerate. But how much does the difference matter?

Looking at numbers can only tell you so much, and having used both phones, I can tell you that the difference isn't noticeable with everyday use. Perhaps if you're a fan of high-octane mobile gaming, or you tend to do a lot of performance-heavy tasks on your phone, then sure, better performance may be needed. Likewise, the S26 Ultra lasted an extra 103 minutes in our battery test, no doubt thanks to the extra energy efficiency of the newer hardware.

Is that enough to warrant the extra price? Possibly not, especially if that money could be better spent elsewhere.

In the past, anyone buying an older phone had to contend with the fact the phone may run out of official software support before they were done with it. Not only does this mean you miss out on newly-released software features, loss of security updates meant your phone was more vulnerable to attacks and other security threats — not to mention the fact that you'll eventually stop being able to use your favorite apps.

In a recent development, these days that's much less of a concern. Companies like Google and Samsung have pledged several years of software support on their devices — with up to seven years support on flagships. Likewise, Apple typically offers five to six years of iOS updates on all devices, and makes a point of releasing critical security updates years after other software support has dried up.

Plus, you'd be surprised at how many phone features are purely software-based. There have been instances where AI features on Samsung and Pixel phones started off as exclusive to the newest flagships, but made their way to older phones in a software revision.

According to recent reports, extended software support isn't available on all phones, and there are a lot of brands that still offer the bare minimum of two Android updates and three years of security support. Mostly this glitch affects budget brands with phones that are typically cheap enough that it makes more sense to buy the latest models — examples include Motorola G Power line and TCL.

It has been revealed that just because you're looking at older phones doesn't mean you should feel pressured into buying used or refurbished models. There are plenty of brand upcoming devices available, but the older the device the less likely you'll be able to find one. That remarked, there are extra advantages to buying a used device instead.

For starters, used and refurbished phones are often significantly cheaper. Refurbished phones are often a little pricier than standard used phones, because their condition has been restored to the point that they're almost as good as new. Some of them even come with warranties, just to give you the extra piece of mind that things aren't likely to go wrong.

Buying a pre-owned device also means that a single phone is getting a upcoming lease on life, and that has a much lower environmental impact. Rather than buying a brand new phone, which involves mining, manufacturing, shipping and all those other industrial processes, you're saving an older phone from going through that same process in reverse. That's a nice bonus considering you're probably more interested in the lower price tag.

The first Apple e-series phone still has a lot of great qualities. A solid camera, good battery life, Apple Intelligence and the power of the A18 chipset.

This entry-level foldable comes with a large 6.9-inch foldable display, a cover display capable of running full Android apps, an assortment of AI features and compact design.

The iPhone 16 is the oldest phone Apple still sells, and it can be had for slightly less — so long as you're happy being locked to Walmart's Straight Talk MVNO. It's got good cameras and performance, as well as full access to Apple Intelligence.

There's no successor to this super slim phone yet, but its age means it's a little cheaper than other Galaxy phones. Plus, unlike the iPhone Air, this one actually has two cameras to work with.

Industry observers note that the Galaxy S25 Ultra is very similar to the the S26 Ultra, though it lacks the fast charging and Privacy Display. Still, you get to enjoy good performance, a bright and sharp display and long battery life, alongside the 200MP camera lens.

It has been revealed that the iPhone air is slim, lightweight and far more durable than it looks. Not to mention the fact it has all the benefits of owning an iPhone like good performance, camera quality and long software support.

Recent findings suggest that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is new, and it's expensive, but last year's model is a good $500 cheaper than the current price. It lacks the crease-free screen and larger battery, but it still offers an excellent viewing experience, battery life and camera performance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After an already-busy 2025, Ethan Hawke has somehow kept up the pace this year with one project after another. Theatrically, he's shared the screen with Russell Crowe in their new historical crime drama The Weight and lent his voice to Andrew Niccol's ambitious animated fantasy I, Object. On the small screen, meanwhile, he once again sought out the truth as the danger-prone Lee Raybon in Season 2 of The Lowdown, and he reprised his role as the Caped Crusader for DC's Batwheels series. Yet, in the middle of all that, he still found the time to launch his first podcast passion project, co-created by his Sinister and The Black Phone partners Scott Derrickson and C. Robert Cargill, and inspired by the AM talk radio days of Art Bell.

Industry observers note that midnight Radio is now halfway through its nine-episode run, and there are yet more eerie calls to take. The serialized supernatural show unfolds in real time, with Hawke taking the lead as the host of a cult-favorite late-night radio show. While used to hearing conspiracy theories and other bizarre claims, one night sends him into a chilling loop when a man claiming to be part of a long-lost U.S. space mission gives his line a ring. Their call opens the floodgates to stories of an entire web of government cover-ups, psychological warfare, and interdimensional breaches, alongside odd signals breaking through the static that raise questions about who, or what, is talking to the host. With such a wide-open theme, each episode brings its fair share of colorful characters with their own curious tales to tell, voiced by a series of big-name stars.

It has been revealed that after previewing the series ahead of its debut, Collider is excited to once again partner with the iHeartPodcasts production and unveil the first listen for Episode 5, "Bone Machine." During this session, the host invites listeners to question whether the dead can communicate with the living through the power of cassette tapes. He has a selection of Electronic Voice Phenomena, or EVPs, to share that supposedly contain the words of the deceased, but there's more than meets the eye. Callers keep ringing in with claims about the existence of a clandestine ring of gambling groups where those recordings are the prize and, supposedly, among them is one so horrifying it not only stands out from the rest, but features the host himself.

In a recent development, four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

It has been revealed that your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Sources indicate that to help parse the strange recordings and discern the voices of the dead within them, Hawke's host will need the help of an expert. Fortunately, he just so happens to have one on hand in the form of Dr. Jill Esteban, played by the Oscar nominee's recent The Lowdown Season 2 co-star, Betty Gilpin. Like Hawke, Gilpin's had a busy 2026, between their neo-noir crime comedy, Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning, and Apple TV's breakout horror comedy darling, Widow's Bay. Fittingly, one of the callers they'll deal with is also played by someone familiar with the island of Katie Dipold's Emmy winner — Hamish Linklater. Known for his time in Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, he voices "Speedy," a shady customer somehow entangled in the seedy ghostly tape trade.

In addition to iHeartPodcasts, Midnight Radio was produced by Ethan and Ryan Hawke's Under The Influence Productions banner, Cargill and Derrickson's Crooked Highway, and Mickey Schiff. Gilpin and Linklater are also just the tip of the iceberg as far as stars go. Noah Centineo, Vincent D’Onofrio, Willa Fitzgerald, Levon Hawke, Austin Pendleton, and Hubert Point-Du Jour were also previously confirmed to be appearing in the series. With four episodes remaining, there may yet be more surprises with spooky stories to share with listeners for those late-night drives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone Duo can do a lot of things: multitasking, note-taking and gaming to name a few. But I've been using it to catch up on my reading list, because the 7.6-inch inner display is perfectly proportioned to replace that upcoming Kindle you may have been eyeing up in Black Friday sales.

The best Kindles, and other ereaders, have always positioned themselves as a distraction-free reading experience: You use them for reading books (or comics) and nothing else. There's some truth to that; I would often pick up the iPhone Duo intending to read a chapter or two during my commute only to be led astray by the siren call of my Duolingo streak or a WhatsApp message that needed replying to.

It has been revealed that not anymore! Thanks to a neat patch to Apple's Shortcuts app that's only available on the iPhone Duo, you can automate a shortcut based on the Duo's folded state. When you pair this with Apple Books (or another reading app), you can stop interruptions or distractions before they happen.

Open the Shortcuts app on your iPhone Duo, and tap the + button in the bottom corner, then tap Edit in the top right corner.

Tap on "Automation" beneath the text box and scroll down until you see the option for "Open or Closed" underneath the "Display" heading. Tap it to add the instruction to your Shortcut.

Navigate back to your Shortcut menu and tap on "Open App". The command will appear on the left-hand pane. Once added, tap the "App" on the left and select Apple Books from the drop-down menu that appears.

Selecting Apple Books will, by default, open the app to your current book. If you want to specify a different command — like seeing opening directly into a curated list of the books you want to read, you can do that by tapping the Apple Books app itself on the right pane and adding the instruction to your list of commands.

Once you've set up this Shortcut, the iPhone Duo will launch directly into your current book when you unfold it. If you want to get back to your home screen, all you need to do is swipe up — but this is a handy little tip for always putting your reading habit first.

10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth.
  • The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.
  • According to recent reports, an isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?).

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

According to recent reports, an isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

Recent findings suggest that the Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

According to recent reports, if you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it massive and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for latest planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

Sources indicate that if you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous fresh reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend states a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.

Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a fresh event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.

This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both key buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.

Additionally, Apple has moved the current month to the top-center of the screen and added the year too. Because the year is now always prominently visible, Apple removed it from the back button in the top-left.

According to recent reports, finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’.

You can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a big difference in everyday use.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I'm an unapologetic Swag Golf fan. I love the limited drops of cool headcovers and golf apparel. Honestly, I'm a sucker for anything ultra-limited. I'm also quick to jump on anything cool that comes in a blind box or bag. The surprise sucks me in every time (and I love great golf gifts in general).

So when I found out one of the best golfers in the world, Bryson DeChambeau (he's also arguably the most famous thanks in part to his massive YouTube channel and its Break 50 series), was partnering with Swag to bring limited mystery headcovers to Dick's Sporting Goods and Golf Galaxy, I was excited.

When I got the chance to talk to DeChambeau himself about the headcovers, I had to find out where the inspiration came from. It turns out we really do "have so much time and so little to do.".

Sources indicate that if you're a fan of Bryson DeChambeau and enjoy a bit of mystery, this is a cool item to snag. Each of the 13 designs features Break 50 logos and fan-chosen designs. Four people also get to meet Bryson, go behind the scenes of a Break 50 episode, hit the range and have lunch with DeChambeau. And even if you don't win, 50 headcovers have his autograph, which gives you something else to chase.

Industry observers note that okay, so officially Willy Wonka has nothing to do with this project, but according to Bryson DeChambeau, "we wanted to give fans an opportunity to experience and feel something different." A blind box isn't new, though. There are lots of products in the golf space (and pop culture in general) that come in blind boxes.

According to recent reports, but this one is a little different: "Being a Willy Wonka fan growing up, we thought there could be something cool with a golden ticket. And that golden ticket turned into a golden headcover with four different tiers.".

In a recent development, the highest tier isn't just an incredibly limited headcover, though. The people who are lucky enough to find one at Dick's or Golf Galaxy actually get to hang out with Bryson. "They're gonna be going behind the scenes with a Break 50. They're going to have lunch with me, and I'm gonna take them to the driving range. We're gonna have a great day.".

Of course, there are other prizes (besides the 13 cool headcovers). There are 50 signed headcovers in the mix, plus there are different tiers of headcovers. Tier 2 features two limited designs that are hard to come by, tier 3 has slightly more common designs, and tier 4 has the most common.

In a recent development, one of the main complications with Swag is that their prices are high, with some headcovers going for more than $100 because they're limited. But this blind bag sells for $59, which is quite reasonable for a high-end headcover. "It's not at a crazy price point, DeChambeau noted. "Eventually, we want to do more stuff at even lower price points," to "grow the game of golf and grow the fan base.".

In a recent development, but if you win, don't expect to hit a shot over Bryson's house during filming. "Insurance would probably not be happy about that," Bryson chuckled when I brought up the idea. It looks like his windows will stay safe... for now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple is rolling out the second developer beta of macOS 27.3 ahead of the official launch of the update, which includes several notable additions. Here’s what’s coming.

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS 27.3 developer beta 1, followed by the public beta a few days later, amid a slew of hardware releases that included new M6-powered iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

And contrary to macOS 27.2, the latest update is shaping up to be pretty significant. In addition to expanding Siri AI support to four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, the system also expands Siri AI’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in apps like Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders.

macOS 27.3 beta 2 also introduces new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and you can read more about that here. This change comes in response to concerns about increasingly capable AI agents gaining broad access to owners’ personal data and control over their Macs.

Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to create advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions, allowing the assistant to coordinate multistep actions across different apps.

According to recent reports, macOS 27.3 also introduces Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari, as well as native Live Activities support in the menu bar. Additionally, macOS 27.3 so far include native Markdown rendering in Quick Look, a newly introduced Pro Light screensaver, and additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through public iCloud links.

The build number for macOS 27.3 Golden Gate developer beta 2 is 26C5047e. We are digging through the system and will report back with what we find.

LG’s 65-inch C6 OLED has the largest dollar discount in this sale at $1,350 off, which brings it from $2,699.99 down to $1,349.99.

There's no guarantee that Cyber Monday will bring lower TV prices, particularly when some of the early Black Friday deals are already offering discounts approaching 50%. Recent findings suggest that that depends on your budget, room size, and how you plan to use it. The LG OLED evo C6 and Samsung S90H are worth considering for movie enthusiasts and gamers who want excellent contrast and smooth motion, while the Hisense U7 and TCL QM64L offer mini-LED alternatives for brighter living rooms. For a large screen at a relatively affordable price, the 75-inch Hisense U6 Pro at $699.99 stands out, while the 65-inch Roku Plus Series at $449.99 makes sense for everyday streaming on a tighter budget. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while Siri AI expanded on what kinds of things you can ask Apple’s voice assistant in many ways, one area where the system took a step back was health data. Since Siri AI’s launch in iOS 27.0, the system has enforced guardrails that do not allow it to access data from the Health app, despite the older Siri Classic being able to do just that.

However, it seems Apple is about to close the gap. In the latest iOS 27.3 beta, just released to developers today, customers are now able to ask their iPhone about health data related questions and Siri AI will answer.

For instance, you can ask about your recent step count or heart rate readings, find out about activity rings progress, log medications and more.

When asking Siri for health stats, the assistant generates a human natural language response and renders a little inline card that uses familiar user interface elements from the Health app. Similarly, if you ask about your activity rings, a visualisation of your activity rings is shown in the chat transcript.

According to recent reports, again, this is catch-up compared to what you’ve been able to do with old Siri for several years at this point. However, empowered by the LLM behind the scenes, you can ask questions about your health data that are a bit more open-ended.

You can also do more complicated requests like ‘Send a message to Chance about the status of my activity rings’, or ‘How many steps am I on track to do this week?’. These are the kind of tasks that old Siri would never be able to do.

Sources indicate that at least on this current build, the upcoming Siri AI Health functionality appears to have been enabled on iOS. It’s currently unclear if the functionality will also be available through watchOS.

iOS 27.3 also introduces a revamped Health app, with a radically latest design that includes new insights, suggestions and views about your health and fitness.

iOS 27.3 is presently in beta and is expected to be released publicly later this year, likely in early December.

Flights, banks, and email keep going down — here’s how to tell if it’s an outage or a cyberattack

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when 52,846 readers told us in our poll that they were hit by the Outlook outage, it was a reminder of just how disruptive a single breakdown can be.
  • Almost every widespread outage often comes down to ordinary human error or fragile infrastructure rather than malicious hacking.
  • If your bank app freezes or your flight gets delayed by a system breakdown, here is how to figure out what is actually going on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when 52,846 readers told us in our poll that they were hit by the Outlook outage, it was a reminder of just how disruptive a single breakdown can be. Anytime an essential service stalls like that, speculation about hackers or a coordinated cyberattack quickly spreads.

The truth is far less dramatic. Almost every widespread outage often comes down to ordinary human error or fragile infrastructure rather than malicious hacking.

If your bank app freezes or your flight gets delayed by a system breakdown, here is how to figure out what is actually going on.

Digital services rely on millions of lines of code and overlapping networks, which means things break constantly.

It has been revealed that most major outages are caused by mundane technical failures and human error, a botched software update, a mistyped setting, a severed underground fiber cable, or a simple power failure. Unless concrete evidence of hacking emerges, an accidental technical error is almost always the safest bet.

In fact, according to the Uptime Institute, human error directly or indirectly contributes to between two-thirds and four-fifths of all data center downtime incidents — and roughly 85 percent of those human-error outages stem from staff failing to follow procedures or flaws in the procedures themselves.

When one major service goes down, it often creates a domino effect that makes other apps look broken too.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

A payment failure at a single large bank can stall transfers at several others, and a single cloud provider outage can knock dozens of unrelated websites offline at once.

Rather than trusting panicked posts on social media, check an independent outage tracker like Downdetector to see if other customers are reporting problems nationwide, or search for the company’s official status page and verified newsroom account.

Major tech platforms, banks, and airlines maintain live dashboards that explain whether their systems are actually offline or just waiting on another partner to come back up.

The timeline of an outage is often one of the biggest clues to its cause.

When an engineer pushes a bad enhancement or a server overloads, companies can usually undo the change, reroute traffic, and restore service within a few minutes or hours — though widespread system crashes can occasionally take longer to untangle.

Deep-seated cyberattacks, such as ransomware breaches, take much longer to resolve because companies have to lock down their networks, investigate the intrusion, kick intruders out, and rebuild damaged systems from scratch, a process that regularly drags on for days or even weeks.

In the first few hours of a major breakdown, nobody, not even the organization experiencing the crash, always knows the exact root cause.

When hackers are behind a major disruption, they often claim credit publicly to demand ransom or score political points, or federal cybersecurity officials eventually confirm a breach after investigating.

Until an affected manufacturer or government agency shares verified findings, patience is the best defense against bad rumors.

iOS 27.3 also brings video podcasts from the Apple Podcasts app into TV.

Sources indicate that as we reported this morning, there’s a dedicated video podcasts section coming to the TV app. But you can also, via your Account Settings, choose to sync playback data from Apple Podcasts.

If you enable sync, then video podcasts played in one app will be added to the queue and playback history in both apps.

Resta la sua obiezione sulla possibilità di votare due volte; alle elezioni del 14 dicembre ci saranno due candidati.

Adriano Galliani rinuncia al ricorso contro l’ammissione della sua candidatura e guarda al voto del 14 dicembre. A margine del Premio Galbiati, ai microfoni di Sky Sport, ha risposto a Giovanni Malagò, commissario straordinario della FIGC, che aveva definito signorile la sua scelta.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM.

Galliani resta convinto della propria posizione: «Continuo ad essere convinto che non si possa dare un voto due volto. Altrimenti qualunque candidatura può essere tolta all'ultimo minuto. All'improvviso ti viene fatta una revoca e cade la candidatura». Spiega così la decisione di fermarsi: «Detto questo faccio calcio da 50 anni, ho pensato che il nostro mondo ha bisogno di serenità, tranquillità, abbiamo tanti problemi, allora ho pensato di non fare niente e andiamo al 14 dicembre».

Alla domanda se la rinuncia renderà più serena la campagna elettorale, risponde: «Assolutamente sì, si vota fra 4 settimane, ci sono due candidati e vedremo cosa succede».

Sources indicate that galliani racconta come ha cambiato idea sulla candidatura: «Avevo detto di no in precedenza. Mi hanno convinto le telefonate, oltre che di qualche club, dell'AssoCalciatori e dell'AssoAllenatori». Aggiunge: «Ulivieri mi ha detto che gli anni migliori per i rapporti con la Lega Calcio, di cui sono stato rappresentante, sono stati secondo lui quando c'ero io. Calcagno mi ha detto il suo maestro, l'avvocato Campana, gli aveva detto a sua volta che i rapporti migliori c'erano quando io ero presidente di Lega. Così mi hanno convinto».

Industry observers note that sul programma dichiara: «È molto lungo, l'ho presentato e depositato. Ora sono qui per premiare la memoria del grande Baresi e vi rimando al programma, non vorrei parlare troppo tempo».

Interpellato sulla Nazionale, Galliani risponde: «Non voglio parlare di Nazionale per evidenti motivi, quindi parliamo di Galbiati». Ricorda di averlo trovato al Milan al suo arrivo nel 1986 e di averlo poi voluto a Monza: «Ha insegnato a calciare a Ibrahimovic. Ibra era fortissimo, ma non sapeva calciare in porta, Italo glielo ha insegnato. Poi da talent scout scovava giocatori, ce ne sono pochi bravi come lui».

  • Sources indicate that one of the best streaming services around, Netflix is packed with romantic miniseries you'll fall for, whether you're after a small-screen adaptation of a beloved romance book, a costume drama set in the greater "Bridgerton" universe, or a Christmas-season charmer full of lovely optimism and holiday cheer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when it comes to the miniseries format, we're used to high-tension genres like true crime, historical drama, psychological thrillers, and family sagas. Finding a short-form series dedicated to romance — where the stakes are more of the will-they-won't-they emotional sort — feels far rarer, but not impossible, as these three great Netflix miniseries prove.

Sources indicate that one of the best streaming services around, Netflix is packed with romantic miniseries you'll fall for, whether you're after a small-screen adaptation of a beloved romance book, a costume drama set in the greater "Bridgerton" universe, or a Christmas-season charmer full of lovely optimism and holiday cheer. And, even better, the critics agree — each of the following demonstrates has an impressive 90% or higher rating on Rotten Tomatoes.

If you're after a sweet, moving love story that plays out across a handful of episodes, here are five Netflix romance miniseries to add to your watchlist.

Based on the bestselling 2009 romance novel by British author David Nicholls, "One Day" charts the slow-burn romance between University of Edinburgh grads Emma Morley and Dexter Mayhew — played by the winning duo of Ambika Mod and Leo Woodall, who share a wonderfully natural, palpable chemistry — over the course of two decades, catching up with the characters on the same date every year.

Over 14 half-hour episodes, we see Emma and Dexter grow up, break up, make up, and try to find their respective places in the world, allowing for heavier things like loss, heartbreak, and healing in a genre that's usually smitten by the lighthearted and breezy.

The romantic drama has a strong 92% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with critics showering particular praise on Mod and Woodall's lead performances. "Chronicling the passage of time with well-observed sweep, 'One Day' is by turns giddy and somber but always swooningly romantic," reads the site's critical consensus.

Stream "One Day" on Netflix now.

It has been revealed that when it comes to Netflix romantic series, few names are bigger than "Bridgerton," the streamer's Regency-era romance following the relationship entanglements and social pressures of the eight Bridgerton siblings. (The show will be back for its steamy fifth season next year.).

Recent findings suggest that but equally swoon-worthy is the "Bridgerton" miniseries "Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story," which serves as a prequel to the O.G. Netflix romance. The six-episode historical drama focuses on the 1761 arranged marriage of 17-year-old Princess Charlotte (a star-making breakthrough performance from India Amarteifio) to King George III (Corey Mylchreest), which kicks off an epic love story that changes the course of England.

Mixing genuine emotional depth with sharp social commentary, "Queen Charlotte" is "a resplendent romance between two of the most interesting characters in the 'Bridgerton saga'" and "a spin-off that arguably perfects the primary series' formula," per the critical consensus on Rotten Tomatoes, where the miniseries has an excellent 94% approval rating.

Stream "Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story" on Netflix now.

Sure, it's not even Thanksgiving yet, but who says we can't get into the Christmas spirit a little early, right? This cheery 2020 rom-com series will help you do just that: Midori Francis ("Saccharine") and Austin Abrams — who has been a bit of a scream king lately, between 2025's "Weapons" and this year's "Resident Evil" —play two Fresh York City teens who develop feelings for each other through traded messages in a shared red notebook, before they ever lay eyes on each other.

Over eight episodes, the youngsters — she, a holiday optimist, and he, a bit of a Christmas Scrooge — challenge each other to step out of their comfort zones through written dares, personal thoughts, and revealed secrets, all set against iconic locations in snowy New York City.

The romance series received the ever-so-rare 100% critical score on Rotten Tomatoes, with critics praising the flick's "charming" lead actors and the overall story as "a delightful rom-com adventure with plenty of holiday cheer.".

Stream "Dash & Lily" on Netflix now.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to macOS 27.3 beta 2, Apple is also rolling out the first Release Candidates for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4. Here are the details.

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS Tahoe 26.7.3 and Sequoia 15.8.3, along with macOS 27.2.1 Golden Gate, all of which included security fixes related to AirPlay, Bluetooth, and Messages, among others.

Today, the company released the first RCs for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4, along with the second developer beta for macOS 27.3.

As is usually the case with direct-to-RC rollouts, Apple’s notes mention only that the updates provide ”security fixes for your Mac.” The actual release notes will likely become available soon after Apple officially releases macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.4 in the coming weeks.

The build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.4 RC 1 is 24H319, and the build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.4 RC 1 is 25G422.

Breaking: MagSafe Monday: MOFT’s Trackable Field Wallet holds eight cards, cash, and supports Find My

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the one thing Apple’s own MagSafe wallet does that a few third-party wallets have is Find My.
  • MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
  • MOFT has been making the origami-style folding wallet for many years, and this model works like any other Find My accessory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the one thing Apple’s own MagSafe wallet does that a few third-party wallets have is Find My. If you misplace your wallet, your iPhone tells you where it is. Most MagSafe wallets either skip tracking entirely or have a pocket for an AirTag, which adds thickness and it’s another thing to buy. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet builds the tracker into the wallet itself, so it indicates up in the Find My app.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

MOFT has been making the origami-style folding wallet for many years, and this model works like any other Find My accessory. So that means you get left-behind alerts when you leave without it, and the ability to make it trackable through Apple’s network if it’s across town instead of under the couch. It also works with Google’s Find Hub on Android, which matters if you’ve got a mixed household of devices.

The wallet is powered by a built-in battery rather than a watch-style battery, and MOFT says a charge lasts about six months. You charge it by placing the wallet on a Qi charger for about an hour and a half, which, in practice, means dropping it on a MagSafe dock twice a year. That’s a better setup than an AirTag in a wallet as well.

The wallet holds up to eight cards, or closer to four to six if you also use the hidden compartment for cash. A pull tab in the wallet brings your everyday cards out in one motion, while your driver’s license and cash stay tucked inside of it. It’s made from MOFT’s vegan leather and at 14 mm thick, it’s slimmer than a traditional wallet but noticeably thicker than Apple’s card-only wallet, which is the price you are going to pay to hold up this much stuff.

According to recent reports, the stand is the usual MOFT origami fold-out, and it works in portrait and landscape for FaceTime or watching a video on the plane. You can buy it without the stand if you’d rather have the thinner version. It comes in Jet Black, Misty Cove, Terracotta, and Peony.

In a recent development, two things to know going in. There’s no RFID blocking in this version (MOFT has a non-Find My Snap Field Wallet if you want that). MOFT also warns that the magnets can affect magnetic-stripe cards, so avoid putting a hotel key in it.

I’ve spent the past month on a Pelican accessory beat, using wallets designed for outdoor use. The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is the other end of that accessory spectrum: more cards, a stand, and Find My built in. If Find My is the reason you’ve stuck with Apple’s wallet, this is a really nice option that holds a bunch and is trackable.

The MOFT Trackable Field Wallet is available on Amazon and directly from MOFT.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you’re hosting over the holiday season and you have a small kitchen, you’re probably racking your brain for more space. Even if you have a decent-sized layout, your countertops can quickly get cluttered with appliances, leaving no room to prep.

That’s why I’m doing a pre-holiday purge and clearing my countertops to give me enough elbow room to work — and these are the only three hard-working appliances that earned their spot.

Every appliance you have staked out on your kitchen countertop takes up precious prep space — and during the holidays, you need every square inch of it. When you’re cooking a feast for a crowd, the last thing you want is the hassle of constantly shuffling gadgets around.

Planning ahead and clearing your countertops before the festive season gets into full swing will ensure the only steam in your kitchen comes from the stove — not from you!

While I am a secret neat freak and would love to have clear countertops, it simply isn’t practical, especially if you enjoy cooking and don’t rely on takeout. But I’ve found from experience, and from cooking a whole stack of festive dinners, that less is really more. That’s why I now keep my countertops reasonably tidy and rely on three main appliances instead of juggling a dozen gadgets.

Recent findings suggest that A stand mixer is always my number one kitchen appliance that stays out on my countertop. And while any stand mixer can help you whip, beat and knead, some have extra powers. #39462. Industry News: Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

Industry News: Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer notes it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • According to recent reports, andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer notes it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

According to recent reports, andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he notes he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to massive concerns in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Recent findings suggest that andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a newly introduced paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

It has been revealed that ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Recent findings suggest that having stated that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of consumers.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

Recent findings suggest that “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

In a recent development, I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and mentioned, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Industry observers note that over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing newly introduced here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one organization or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that demonstrated up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Industry observers note that ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from massive data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

Recent findings suggest that when you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having remarked that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For massive data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

According to recent reports, for example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very promptly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Sources indicate that ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Sources indicate that ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention swiftly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Recent findings suggest that ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Recent findings suggest that ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion people. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these problems more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a organization approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

It has been revealed that ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

Industry observers note that how do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Industry observers note that ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift glitch. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and revision the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In a recent development, in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion people. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

In a recent development, ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

According to recent reports, ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

While it was obvious that the number of iPhone Duo-ready apps would increase over time, their limited availability was a big part of the conversation around early reviews and online commentary in the first days after the device launched.

That said, it was clear even from the early reviews that app updates were picking up quickly, with some reviewers having to rewrite or re-record parts of their coverage as more apps gained support for the device.
