Industry News: The Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited's TMR sticks, Hall Effect triggers and Command screen make it the pro PS5 controller I’ve been waiting for

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it didn’t take long for the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited to earn a permanent spot in my PS5 setup.
  • Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
  • The Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited is one of the best PS5 controllers today, period.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it didn’t take long for the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited to earn a permanent spot in my PS5 setup. Fitted with TMR thumbsticks and dual-mode Hall Effect triggers, the R5U delivers pro-grade performance and gives you a competitive edge across a range of genres. It features a built-in screen for on-the-fly customization, and you can customize its hardware, too. Oh, and the controller is very comfortable and ergonomic. Though I wish its battery life was longer and the omission of some features made me miss the DualSense, these minor flaws are overshadowed by everything else the R5U offers.

Chunky, comfortable and ergonomic.

TMR sticks for pro-grade precision.

Extremely customizable (hardware and software).

Lacks native DualSense features (naturally).

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited is one of the best PS5 controllers today, period. That’s the review. My job here is done. I jest, I jest! The R5U is simply phenomenal, whether you’re a casual or competitive esports gamer. Supremely precise TMR thumbsticks, dual-mode Hall Effect triggers, and plenty of customizable buttons, packed into an ergonomic body make the R5U extremely easy to recommend.

It has been revealed that in addition to that, the R5U comes fitted with a built-in screen for on-the-fly customization as well as a dock for simultaneously charging and displaying the controller. It naturally lacks DualSense features, like haptic feedback, and battery life is limited to just 10 hours. Are either of those dealbreakers? Not in the slightest.

Sources indicate that the R5U is a great step-up for those who own just the first-party DualSense. It’s a pro gamepad through and through. For the complete breakdown, read my full Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited review.

2.4GHz wireless, Bluetooth, USB-C wired.

From its superb TMR thumbsticks and Hall Effect triggers to its degree of software and hardware customization, the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited is a formidable controller for PS5 players.

It has been revealed that it wouldn’t be a pro-grade controller if it utilized traditional analog thumbsticks. The Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited is fitted with TMR (or Tunnel Magneto Resistance) thumbsticks, which achieve greater precision than their Hall Effect counterparts by using weak electromagnetic waves. TMR sensors can detect even the most minute movements — perfect for competitive gaming.

The R5U is one of a handful of PS5 controllers to feature TMR sticks, like the Razer Raiju V3 Pro ($219), but I want every gamepad to have it. Of course, the R5U won’t make you better at esports overnight, but the TMR sticks’ precision is truly unmatched. I tested the controller by playing 007 First Light, Need for Speed Heat, and Ghost of Yotei on my PS5 Slim, and I was thoroughly impressed with the R5U.

Proving responsive and accurate across all three titles, I appreciated being able to fine-tune my movements exactly the way I wanted. In 007 First Light, I was able to execute precise headshots while taking cover — multiple ones in succession, too, as the R5U’s sticks start and stop without any hiccups. Similarly, in Need for Speed Heat, I was able to make subtle steering corrections when racing at 200+ mph without overcorrecting or spinning out.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In a recent development, TMR sticks (as well as Hall Effect ones) are also more durable than traditional analog thumbsticks, and they’re resistant to stick drift. As someone who has lost many controllers to it, that alone makes the R5U a worthy investment.

Industry observers note that alongside TMR thumbsticks, the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited features dual-mode Hall Effect triggers. Using the buttons on the R5U’s back, you can swap between two trigger modes: full-range long presses for millimeter-precise travel, and short microswitch clicks for mouse-like controls. In Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, I opted for short clicks as it meant that I only needed to tap R2 to initiate a Gradient Counter.

According to recent reports, similarly, when parkouring in Ghost of Yotei, I was able to instantly throw my grapple hook mid-jump, and swiftly attack enemies with my throwable weapons. Meanwhile, in the likes of Need for Speed Heat, I kept the triggers set to full-range for an immersive accelerating and braking experience.

It has been revealed that I also love the R5U’s face and back buttons. There are four back buttons (and two top ones) in total and you can use the built-in Command screen to assign your preferred actions to these (more on that shortly).

It has been revealed that these microswitches feel snappy, and I’d argue that their responsiveness is on par with that of the Razer Raiju V3 Pro. The R5U’s back and face buttons take things a bit further as they provide a more cushioned, ergonomic feel than the Raiju V3 Pro. All in all, the R5U delivers a wonderful gaming experience.

Now that I’ve talked about the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited’s gaming chops, let’s talk about its design and build. The R5U is an extremely comfortable and ergonomic controller. Even after a six-hour gaming session, I didn’t experience any discomfort or cramping. That’s thanks to the R5U’s chunky grips and rounded, contoured shape that’s similar to the Razer Raiju V3 Pro.

Measuring 6.3 x 4.13 x 2.36 inches, the R5U is almost the same size as the DualSense Edge ($200) and the Turtle Beach Victrix Pro BFG Reloaded ($209). At 10.5oz, it’s lighter than the former but slightly heavier than the latter. I prefer heavier pads as they feel substantial to hold, and I’ve thoroughly enjoyed using the R5U. No complaints here.

Sources indicate that as it’s officially licensed by PlayStation, the R5U features PlayStation Shapes face buttons. Surprisingly, though, it features offset asymmetrical thumbsticks, similar to what you’d find on Xbox controllers. Personally, I find asymmetrical sticks more comfortable than symmetrical ones, like on the first-party DualSense and DualSense Edge.

Recent findings suggest that I love the DualSense and I’ve grown so accustomed to using the central touchpad which, in my opinion, makes games like Ghost of Yotei feel extremely immersive. Third-party controllers don’t usually feature a multi-touch surface similar to that, but the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited foregoes it completely.

Industry observers note that instead, you’ll find a built-in 1.8-inch Command screen for on-the-fly customization, and I found it extremely useful and handy. To activate the screen, you need to press the round Multi-Function button located between the triggers. You can then use the X and O face buttons to navigate the screen and adjust audio, thumbstick settings and button mapping.

In a recent development, I thoroughly appreciated being able to adjust the sticks’ dead zones, as well as audio mixing as and when needed. You can also use the screen to remap buttons and assign different actions to the six extras. There are eight profiles you can then save these settings to, so for racing games, I assigned nitrous and handbrake to the back buttons so that I could keep my right thumb on the right stick at all times.

The only things you can’t do via the Command screen is change the right stick’s RGB lighting ring, adjust stick response curves, and gyroscope axes customization. For that, you’ll need the R5U Navigator app, available on iOS and Android. The app sports a clean interface and makes quick work of making these adjustments and saving them to the controller’s memory.

Industry observers note that the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited offers good hardware customization. Included in the R5U’s box, you’ll find a plastic case with six joystick heads (two convex, two concave, and two raised concave), six weights (two 10g, two 14g, and two 16g), four stick travel rings, and two interchangeable D-pads (4- and 8-way).

Industry observers note that the weights can be popped into the controller’s grips to give it more heft, and the travel rings can be placed under the thumbsticks for resistance or limiting range of motion. All of these make the R5U feel feature-rich, but it’s worth noting that the Turtle Beach Victrix Pro BFG Reloaded is even more modular with its 11 interchangeable components. Still, it’s nice to see Nacon offer a decent level of hardware customization.

There isn’t a lot wrong with the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited, but it’s worth noting that its battery life isn’t very impressive, and some native DualSense features are absent.

Despite its name, the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited’s battery life is, in fact, not unlimited. It’s officially rated for 10 hours only. Whether that’s good or bad depends on how you look at it. Even at just 10 hours, the R5U has both the first-party PlayStation DualSense and the DualSense Edge beat. Neither have official battery ratings but in our experience, you can squeeze out about 7 hours out of the DualSense and a measly 5 hours out of the DualSense Edge.

Industry observers note that but throw in third-party controllers and the R5U doesn’t sound nearly as impressive. The Turtle Beach Victrix Pro BFG Reloaded can last up to 20 hours, while the Razer Raiju V3 Pro is rated for 36 hours. You’ve also got a gamepad like the SteelSeries Aeon Pro ($259) with its zero downtime battery system (though SteelSeries is yet to release a PS5 edition). So yes, the R5U’s 10-hour battery life is decent but it’s far from the best.

I’m going to preface this point by saying that this isn’t a major con or drawback of the Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited — it’s a natural omission because it isn’t a first-party PS5 controller. As a third-party gamepad, the R5U doesn’t feature haptic feedback or adaptive triggers, just like the Razer Raiju V3 Pro and the Turtle Beach Victrix Pro BFG Reloaded. There’s no central touchpad either (like on the DualSense), as it’s replaced by a built-in settings screen.

There’s no built-in microphone either, so you might want to grab one of the best gaming headsets, like the Razer BlackShark V3 Pro ($249), to communicate with other players. While it would have been great to have these features for a fully immersive gaming experience, it’s a limitation of third-party controllers.

The Nacon Revolution 5 Unlimited isn’t necessarily a groundbreaking controller, and it doesn’t do things very differently from the likes of the Razer Raiju V3 Pro and the Turtle Beach Victrix Pro BFG Reloaded… but that doesn’t mean you should write it off.

Sources indicate that thanks to its TMR thumbsticks and dual-mode Hall Effect triggers, the R5U delivers supreme precision across genres, and it’s a formidable pro-grade PS5 controller. Its chunky grips are extremely comfortable, and its weight is easily adjustable. Software customization is extensive, and the Command screen enables you to adjust the R5U’s settings without diving into its companion app.

According to recent reports, while I don’t believe the R5U will replace my DualSense as the primary controller (as it lacks haptic feedback and adaptive triggers), it’s a serious gamepad for competitive gaming. If you need precision above all else, Nacon’s offering is well worth the money.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.

Recent findings suggest that beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

Sources indicate that at the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

It has been revealed that within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with Newly introduced York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he claims, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

Sources indicate that what’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” notes Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”.

At Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies.

In a recent development, this ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

Industry observers note that among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

To that end, the company is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta states its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO.

In a recent development, “We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” notes Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

Industry observers note that 3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The organization is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby says the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, Upcoming York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.Beta TechnologiesBecause individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont Beta TechnologiesAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company at the moment employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

In a recent development, electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

Sources indicate that that helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

Sources indicate that in Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Recent findings suggest that kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the company’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies.

Industry observers note that by contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

It has been revealed that while the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

Recent findings suggest that “One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” states Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them massive. This limitation is from the batteries.”.

In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

According to recent reports, beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

According to recent reports, the burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

Industry observers note that on Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

It has been revealed that the modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

According to recent reports, what sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

Sources indicate that for instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The firm has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

According to recent reports, beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The organization uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies.

Sources indicate that further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the company’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one key difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

In a recent development, for charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Sources indicate that back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

Then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

  • Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

Sources indicate that with today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a fresh feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:.

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Recent findings suggest that previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the new face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

In a recent development, after updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the newly introduced face unlock feature.

Amazon still has this limited-edition vinyl release available online.

Latest Update: The first ping from Tonga (1997)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Colo

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In January 1997, we sent a ping from the Kingdom of Tonga and got a reply.
  • Sources indicate that when I began spending time in the Kingdom of Tonga in the early 90s, Cable & Wireless was the monopoly telco, international calls costing US$3 per minute to anywhere outside of Tonga.
  • Sources indicate that the telco monopoly had rotten infrastructure, an ancient troposcatter system unreliably serving the outer island of Vava'u, where my friend Commander Goldstern lived.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In January 1997, we sent a ping from the Kingdom of Tonga and got a reply. The Kingdom finally had a permanent connection to the internet, 64 kb/s over a satellite link. Getting there had involved an assortment of secondhand hardware, improvised networks, a Crown Prince, and some unauthorized climbing on rooftops.

Sources indicate that when I began spending time in the Kingdom of Tonga in the early 90s, Cable & Wireless was the monopoly telco, international calls costing US$3 per minute to anywhere outside of Tonga. Spendy even for tourists, beyond exorbitant for locals. You'd queue, and when your turn came, sit in a little booth and the operator would connect you.

Sources indicate that the telco monopoly had rotten infrastructure, an ancient troposcatter system unreliably serving the outer island of Vava'u, where my friend Commander Goldstern lived. He and other people with businesses in Vava'u were sick of the poor communication, so in 1995 I bought a couple of Telebit Trailblazer modems at some surplus place in Silicon Valley and flew up to Vava'u with one and a server running an early RedHat crammed in Goldstern's Lake Buccaneer.

People could then dial into our fax server in Vava'u and the Trailblazers would get the fax data down to Tongatapu. At 19.2 kb/s, but reliably. My SGI Indigo in Sausalito would dial out to Tonga hourly using some sort of scammy, cheap, long-distance expired card service, and retrieve the fax data from our server in Tongatapu. Once in California, the faxes would be forwarded to their destinations.

In a recent development, why a "secretary service"? Well... it was not legal to run a communication firm without a license.

Of course, these regular dialup connections also allowed me to transfer UUCP email. I set up a public email cafe in Tongatapu using a large pile of dumb NCD X-terminals, sourced at magnificent RA Enterprises near the San Jose airport. Lines for the email cafe formed around the block, as the price charged for an hour of email, one pa'anga, was far less than what Cable & Wireless charged for a minute of telephony.

By 1995, I had been delegated the .TO ccTLD by Jon Postel, as that was appropriate for email from Tonga. I asked, he delegated it. And by April 1996 we had DNS running, and a couple of machines online in the Consulate in SF.

Recent findings suggest that crown Prince Tupouto'a ("HRH") and I had become friends. HRH traveled extensively, always staying at the finest hotels, and was well aware of the potential of the internet.

The manager of Cable & Wireless in the Kingdom of Tonga, Jon Morris, said nobody in Tonga would ever want the internet. But nevertheless, at HRH's urging, Jon relented and awarded me a meagre contract to bring in the necessary equipment to attach to their C-band earthstation for an internet link. So my friend Eric Lyons and I hauled in from California various crates of servers running RedHat 3.0.3 and a Cisco 2501 router. I recall it started on a single 64 kb/s space segment. Gratuitously, it was mango season, and we stuffed ourselves with ripe hot mangoes as they dropped from a magnificent tree outside the earthstation.

In a recent development, the photo at the head of this post is the Cable & Wireless machine room in January 1997 shortly after our first ping, the first IP packet sent from the Kingdom over the C-band internet connection, a moment of jubilation. Everything before that, including our fax and UUCP systems, ran through modems over analog telephone circuits. The Kingdom had never previously had an IP connection.

And it didn't take long for others to notice.

Of course, HRH wanted the internet in his bedroom, as one does.

Sources indicate that the tallest building in town was the four-story Reserve Bank building. I bought a couple of early PairGain Megabit Modem 768 HDSL modems and over semi-rotten copper twisted pair in the ground managed to get 768 kb/s symmetric from the Cable & Wireless earthstation to the Reserve Bank building.

With the help of a small commando team from Tonga Defense, one afternoon we installed a small parabolic antenna on the roof of the bank building. And with a pair of unamplified Digital Wireless Corporation WIT-2400 frequency-hopping radio modems managed to establish a surprisingly reliable link about six kilometers from the roof of the bank building to HRH's Italianate villa. We were amazed that 100 milliwatts would work over six kilometers, even with line of sight. Why use the military for the antenna installation? Well, that was easier than getting permission from the governor of the Reserve Bank, who the next morning loudly objected to what he saw as an ugly antenna.

Sources indicate that as an aside, I almost fell 4 stories off the roof of the Reserve Bank when I touched the live JOCV HF antenna. I still have scars on my ass from where the bolts attaching the metal roofing stopped my slide.

Tonga had gone from US$3 per minute operator-connected international calls to a permanent internet link in only a few years. The improvised fax and UUCP systems were obsolete almost immediately, which was exactly the outcome we'd been trying to achieve.

According to recent reports, we'd managed to connect Tonga to the internet. Next, we discovered that its DNS namespace might be worth rather more than the satellite connection itself. But that's another story, one that is already well documented:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buckle up, and try not to get carjacked. After 13 years and back-to-back delays, the excruciating wait for Grand Theft Auto VI has finally come to an end. As the clock struck midnight on Nov. 19, the most anticipated video game of all time officially launched, opening up the neon-soaked streets of Vice City for millions of players on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

According to recent reports, by the way, that “millions” isn’t an understatement. With pre-orders live since June, and the ability to pre-download the game on Nov. 10 driving a surge in early purchases, it’s estimated that over 17 million copies sold prior to launch day. Potentially raking in over $1.6 billion before it’s even available to play, that puts GTA VI over halfway to the lifetime grosses of blockbuster movies like Avengers: Endgame and Avatar (both over $2.9 billion) — well on track to fulfill the expectation of being the largest single media launch ever.

And although it’s already raking in cash for the game’s publisher, Take-Two Interactive, the launch of GTA VI and the subsequent days to follow could potentially be some of the least productive for companies outside of major holidays. A recent IGN poll highlights thousands of fans are planning to take paid time-off or sick days to play the game, something Take-Two CEO, Strauss Zelnick, joked about back in April. But it’s more than just a meme on social media; major corporations like Logitech have actually declared the release date a company-wide holiday.

But if you’re not one of the early adopters, or are on the fence about diving into the zeitgeist, there’s plenty of information already available about what to expect from gaming’s once-white whale.

Like its predecessors, GTA VI is an open-world crime odyssey where players take on the role of fledgling gangsters looking to make their mark on the underworld. As with most mainline entries, the characters and plot are mostly independent from previous installments, but it’s still set in the same satirical take on the U.S.. This time around, the primary setting is in the fictional state of Leonida — a stand-in for Florida — and includes a modern version of the Miami-inspired locale of Vice City. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

This fresh installment is unique in that it follows two protagonists, the Bonnie and Clyde-like duo of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. The latter is a substantial deal for the franchise, marking the first female protagonist for the series. The story begins with Lucia being newly released from prison, reuniting with her paramour to stumble back into a life of crime. Early details indicate that Jason and Lucia’s relationship is the beating heart of GTA VI, and players’ decisions can heavily impact how the two interact. Maintaining a good standing could be critical to surviving the mean streets of Vice City over the course of the game’s runtime, reportedly spanning anywhere from 70 to over 100 hours.

It has been revealed that right now! The game has been available to download for pre-orders since Nov 10., and has been fully available since midnight eastern time in North America. The North America part is key, too. Instead of having a unified global release, GTA VI’s rolling launch granted early access to players worldwide at 12 a.m. local time by region, meaning customers in Oceania and Asia got nearly a full day’s headstart ahead of their U.S. counterparts. To get in completely blind, it’s best to avoid social media. Spoilers are already circulating online.

Like its 2013 predecessor, the new GTA is starting its life cycle as a timed console exclusive, currently available for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. As expected, the divide between PlayStation and Xbox players leans heavily toward the former, with approximately 75 percent of users being on PS5. PC gamers have once been left out in the cold, with no release date currently set outside of consoles. Sadly, Nintendo’s Switch 2 has also been snubbed, despite its rapidly expanding audience driving mature games like Call of Duty back to the platform after a yearslong hiatus. Related Content Lana Del Rey, Dua Lipa, Zara Larsson Contribute New Music to ‘GTA VI: The Album’ Everything We Know About ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ James Bond’s Brightest Future Could Be in Video Games A History of Mario, Nintendo’s Golden Boy.

Recent findings suggest that the Standard Edition of GTA VI costs $79.99, which is technically the base game, plus some extra cosmetic goodies if you’ve pre-ordered. But there’s a catch. Unlike most standard editions which can be upgraded to premium for extra content down the line, the core version simply cuts off access to in-game stores and accessories in the main game. Virtual locations like Electric Fang Tattoo Parlor and One-Eyed Willie’s Mod Shop still exist, but their doors are closed without purchasing the Ultimate Edition ($99.99) — which really makes a hundred bucks the real cost to play GTA VI in its entirety. In fact, the Ultimate Edition is the one immediately offered on digital storefronts, with players needing to toggle to the cheaper one to find it.

On that note, a digital storefront on PlayStation or Xbox will be an essential part of accessing GTA VI. Although you can buy a “physical” box in stores, the purchase doesn’t come with a disc. Instead, in-store versions come with vouchers for a digital download, meaning it’s indistinguishable from buying it on your console. It also means you’ll need to set aside both over 210GB of space on your device to download it, as well as the time to do it. If your internet connection isn’t up to snuff, you could be waiting a few hours after buying the game before you can play it.

There’s no overwhelming benefit to playing on any specific platform, but there are some differences depending on which console and model you own. On both PS5 and Xbox Series X, the game’s visuals target 30 frames-per-second, which is the baseline for modern AAA releases. Although many newer releases get heavily upgraded fidelity or performance on the more expensive PS5 Pro, GTA VI offers slightly enhanced graphics, including better lighting effects and exclusive ray-tracing shadows, with the device’s PSSR (PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution) improving overall image quality. Both base PS5 and Pro consoles will include haptic feedback integration on DualSense controllers, and spatial audio via Sony’s Tempest 3D technology.

The Xbox Series X appears to run the game just as well as the base PS5, although GTA VI will also be accessible to stream via Xbox Cloud Gaming, meaning it can even be played on the last-gen Xbox One. The caveat here is that Xbox Cloud Gaming caps streaming time based on your subscription blueprint (15 hours per month at the highest tier), meaning you won’t get much time in-game if it’s not downloaded to your device. Rockstar also states that the cloud version is based on the specs of the Series S, implying the more affordable of Xbox’s two current consoles has weaker performance.

According to recent reports, one thing you won’t be doing is playing GTA VI online with friends. At launch, the upcoming game is strictly a single-player only experience, with a multiplayer patch expected to come down the line. Trending Stories John Mayer Transports Michael J. According to reviews, yes. The buzz thus far has been enormous, with Rockstar Games’ record for acclaimed games fully intact. GTA VI currently has a Metacritic score of 99, making it the highest-rated video game of all time. On top of that, Grand Theft Auto VI has already received eight nominations at The Game Awards 2026, including Game of the Year — revealed two full days before 99.9 percent of people have even played it.

So, if all of this sounds like your jam, it’s time to put life on pause and dive into the criminal underworld, lest you be left behind.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that germany and Austria are calling for a strategic shift in the ownership of TikTok’s European arm, proposing that it be brought under European management.
  • In a joint statement, representatives of both countries expressed their desire to introduce a corporate structure that guarantees regional oversight of the platform’s algorithms and user data, separating it from its current parent company, Beijing-based ByteDance.
  • The proposal, described by Germany’s Minister for Culture and Media, Wolfram Weimer, and Austria’s State Secretary for Digital Affairs, Alexander Pröll, as an attempt to ‘Europeanise’ the service, is seeking support from other EU member states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that germany and Austria are calling for a strategic shift in the ownership of TikTok’s European arm, proposing that it be brought under European management. In a joint statement, representatives of both countries expressed their desire to introduce a corporate structure that guarantees regional oversight of the platform’s algorithms and user data, separating it from its current parent manufacturer, Beijing-based ByteDance. The proposal, described by Germany’s Minister for Culture and Media, Wolfram Weimer, and Austria’s State Secretary for Digital Affairs, Alexander Pröll, as an attempt to ‘Europeanise’ the service, is seeking support from other EU member states. advertisement   The move follows a similar precedent set in January, when the United States reached an agreement with ByteDance to establish a joint venture in which American interests hold a majority stake in the app’s domestic operations. The concept was first introduced by Minister Weimer, who suggested that a consortium of European media companies could take over the platform’s regional operations. The main motivations behind the move are to safeguard personal data and limit external influence on public debate. Both officials pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the Chinese government’s potential access to European user data, given ByteDance’s origins. They also stressed that, since recommendation systems largely determine the visibility and distribution of content, bringing the platform under European ownership would provide essential control over both its technological framework and customers’ privacy. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (492 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • It has been revealed that as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • In a recent development, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

It has been revealed that as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

In a recent development, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that manufacturer or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

Industry observers note that next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

Sources indicate that once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, patch the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

Face unlock is a good compromise for the iPhone Duo – now let’s have it for the Mac

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Apple first confirmed Face ID, the manufacturer talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.
  • Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….
  • According to recent reports, the first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Apple first confirmed Face ID, the manufacturer talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security ….

According to recent reports, the first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

Recent findings suggest that it took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

Meantime, in 2017 Apple released Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple said at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

Face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

Industry observers note that given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the company is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:.

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

According to recent reports, I do not see any downside provided the feature is off by default and only those who want it will turn it on. Presumably with an explanation of the reasons it gives reduced security.

For myself, I have got so used to using touch ID on my keyboard that I'd likely not make use of it in my business. If anything goes wrong with client information, I want to know, and be able to demonstrate, that I have taken security seriously.

There’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. Currently, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook users have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

What’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

It has been revealed that I’ll let you in on a not-so-well-kept secret about commerce journalism: Every year, we’re sent hundreds of sample products to test for our roundups and reviews. It’s one of the best parts of the job because a) who doesn’t love free stuff, and b) come the holidays, we know the best Christmas gifts almost as well as the guy in the North Pole.

The two most vital qualities to consider when deciding on a gift are usability and uniqueness. The best Christmas gifts can be heavy on one or the other or a mix of both. At one end of the spectrum, you have highly usable presents, like a great pair of earbuds or a streaming subscription. In the middle are useful items that your giftee might not buy for themselves, like a coffee membership or a latest jacket. And on the other far end of the spectrum are things that might not be “useful,” but they’re fun and unique enough to brighten a loved one’s holidays (like this little guy).

Recent findings suggest that for our list of the best Christmas gifts below, we included products across that whole spectrum at all price points, which means there should be something for everyone on your list from acquaintances to close friends and family members. We included our favorite stuff, but also consulted search data throughout the year to predict popular products that your loved ones might be thinking about.

It has been revealed that one of our must-buys for anyone seeing live music is a pair of Loop earplugs. They reduce the noise of concerts down to a safe level, and they look great doing it.

Trade Coffee ensures your loved one gets a new bag of beans or grounds delivered regularly. This means their coffee quality will almost certainly go up (Trade sources some great stuff), but it’s also a fun way to explore new brands they might not normally seek out.

Recent findings suggest that sweaters are a Christmas classic for good reason. But this cashmere quarter-zip from Nordstrom is one they’ll actually wear, whether to the office or around the house.

Cozy Earth’s buttery-soft pajama sets have earned them a cult following that we’re certainly part of. If you’re looking to upgrade a loved one’s sleepwear, it’s an easy present.

It has been revealed that our writer Sophie Dunne gifted her mom a MasterClass membership years ago, and it has made Christmas a breeze: Every year, her mom just wants her subscription renewed. But Sophie’s mom isn’t alone in loving MasterClass. The online learning platform has a course for everyone, whether they’re looking to improve a specific skill or check out something new.

In a recent development, greener pastures await those who diverge from AirPods. One of the best pairs of noise-canceling earbuds on the market are these Momentum 5s from Sennheiser. Funkycache: A Python library to cache functions in SQLite

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alexwlchan

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that six months ago, I wrote an SQLite-backed cache to speed up the build system for this site.
  • It supported getting and setting strings, with a namespace for different functions, and not much else:.
  • This showed the value of a cache, but it provided cache storage, not cache logic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that six months ago, I wrote an SQLite-backed cache to speed up the build system for this site. A static site generator is an ideal candidate for caching, because there are lots of steps that have deterministic behaviour and no side effects. On a site with hundreds of pages, even a few milliseconds per step adds up to a meaningful improvement.

That first cache was fairly basic. It supported getting and setting strings, with a namespace for different functions, and not much else:.

This showed the value of a cache, but it provided cache storage, not cache logic. If I wanted to cache a function, I had to write per-function logic for saving values to the cache and retrieving them later. A lot of that code was tricky to test, and broken in subtle ways. I was so unsure of this code that I deleted the cache whenever I built the site for publication.

In a recent development, I wanted something better, so last week I wrote funkycache, a latest library that encapsulates all of my caching logic, and is much easier to use and test. It can store arbitrary Python objects as both inputs and outputs, and the interface is much simpler for the caller.

To cache a function, you create a FunkyCache instance and add a decorator to your function:.

This is modelled after functools.cache in the standard library. The output of the expensive function is written to an SQLite database, so it’s available after the Python process exits.

Industry observers note that the cache tries to be smart about invalidations. If the source file containing expensive_function changes, the cache for that function is invalidated and will be rebuilt on the next call.

You can also specify a dependency on other files and static values, changes to which will also trigger a cache invalidation:.

In a recent development, when writing funkycache, I wanted to spend a week thinking hard about caching logic, test it thoroughly, then not think about it again for months. You should be able to use funkycache without understanding how it works – but if you’d like to, that’s what I’ll explain in the rest of this post.

If you’d like to try it yourself, funkycache is on PyPI, and the source code is on this website.

The cache is meant for functions which always produce the same output for a given input, so the inputs are the cache key. When we decorate a function, we can see the arguments passed on each call:.

This doesn’t account for different styles of calling the same function – for example, positional versus keyword arguments, or omitting or overriding default arguments.

To get a complete, consistent set of arguments, I use the inspect module:.

This gives me a Python dictionary of the complete set of arguments to the function, which is the same regardless of the calling style.

Python dictionaries aren’t hashable, so they can’t be used as the keys in dictionaries, nor can they be used as keys in SQLite databases. We need to serialise them as a string or byte sequence.

I considered two options for this serialisation: pickle and JSON. In my limited testing, JSON was faster than pickle, so that’s what I chose. Using JSON also gave me more flexibility for speeding up the serialisation.

My initial serialisation was a naive json.dumps call, with a couple of options to ensure consistent ordering and handle types that the standard library doesn’t know how to encode:.

When I started using funkycache, this encoding step swiftly emerged as the slowest part, so I started “reducing” the arguments to make this step faster. This reduction included:.

These are all lossy transformations, but that’s fine for a cache key – we never need to retrieve the original value. It’s theoretically possible for different values to get a colliding hash key, but at my scale it’s unlikely. (A clean build of my site only uses 32,000 keys.).

Sources indicate that the functions in my static site generator are processing things like the content of articles, so individual function arguments might be kilobytes in size. You can use multi-kilobytes keys with SQLite, but you probably shouldn’t – you take a performance hit for larger keys.

I wrote a small benchmark to compare three approaches: storing the JSON-encoded arguments directly, hashing them with MD5, and hashing them with XXH64. The results are a wash for small key sizes, but for larger keys XXH64 is significantly faster, and MD5 is slower than storing the keys directly in SQLite:.

Based on this benchmark, funkycache hashes the JSON cache key with XXH64 before inserting it into SQLite.

In a recent development, the xxHash class of hashing algorithms was a pleasant discovery for me during this project. They are explicitly designed to be fast, not cryptographically secure. Previously I’d used MD5 for this purpose, because it’s widely available and I conflated “weak” with “fast”. Actually running a benchmark revealed my mistake.

Recent findings suggest that serialising cache keys can be a one-way operation, but cached values need to be retrievable. For this, I’m using the inspect module to get the return type from the cached function, then handing the serialisation to Pydantic.

I use type hints and type annotations for all of my Python, so this information is guaranteed to be present. This wouldn’t work with untyped Python, but it’s good enough for me.

Recent findings suggest that the alternative is using pickle, which can store arbitrary Python objects. I wouldn’t have to worry about the security risks because I’d only ever be pickling and unpickling trusted data, but I continued with JSON because I’m already using it for cache keys, and it’s easier to debug.

One of the functions I wanted to cache is a lazy generator, which was a little trickier.

Using functools.cache will cache the generator object, so every call gets the same generator instance, and they all step together. This strikes me as potentially confusing:.

funkycache takes a different approach: it materialises the generator into a list, and stores that list. When it’s retrieved, the list is converted back into a generator by wrapping it with iter.

Industry observers note that to protect against unbounded memory use from a large or infinite generator, there’s a soft memory budget. If the materialised list exceeds this budget, I stop gathering the output in the list and don’t save anything to the cache. The list and any subsequently generated items are passed directly from the original function to the caller.

Some of the functions in my static site generator depend on the contents of template files. When those files change, I want to invalidate the cache and rebuild the pages that use those templates.

When you register a function with funkycache, you can specify a list of files or folders that it depends on:.

funkycache will read the contents of each of those files, and include them in the cache key. When a file changes, it re-evaluates the list of files and decides whether to keep or invalidate the cache.

It has been revealed that I decided not to put any file change tracking in funkycache itself. I already have code for that, and I wanted to keep this project small and focused.

According to recent reports, A function’s cache can also be based on static values. I use this to include the version of vital libraries, so the cache gets invalidated when I upgrade the library. Here’s a short example:.

This project started because I was thinking about reactive programming.

Reactive programming is a bit like using a spreadsheet. You have input cells where you enter data, and other cells that read that data and automatically patch when the inputs change. Those cells can be inputs to other cells, and so on.

It has been revealed that imagine building a static site: your Markdown files act as input cells, and your rendered HTML pages are the dependent cells. Your tasks form a directed acyclic graph (DAG), and updates propagate through the graph.

Industry observers note that for example, in the diagram above, when article1.md changes, the system knows it needs to rebuild article1.html and ripples that patch to list_of_articles.html. But because there’s been no change in their inputs, the tasks to render articles 2 and 3 don’t run at all.

When done correctly, this can be a very efficient style of programming, because steps only ever run if there’s been a change in their inputs.

Industry observers note that there are tools that will do this for you, like Apache Airflow, but I wanted to build my own. My website is a sandbox where I like building things myself as a learning exercise, rather than using somebody else’s library.

Sources indicate that I spent several weeks trying to design an API, but I couldn’t come up with something satisfactory. However, I experimented with a decorator-based API, and that led me to build funkycache, which delivers a lot of the benefits with less fo the complexity.

It has been revealed that building my website with a warm cache now takes about half a second, and a significant chunk of that time is spent traversing the file system for Markdown files. I have ideas for speeding up that step as well, but that’s a task for another day.

funkycache is only a few hundred lines of code, including tests. If this problem sounds interesting, I encourage you to read it, even if it’s not a library you expect to use.

This story was produced in partnership with Deep South Today, a network of nonprofit, nonpartisan local newsrooms in Louisiana, Mississippi, and Arkansas.

An old Dodge pickup sat parked on the street in Zachary, Louisiana, a small city about 16 miles north of Baton Rouge. Two figures clad in black slipped out into the warm July night: a young man and a girl. Jace Crehan was 21, muscular and stocky with a youthful face and cropped dark hair. Brittany Monk was 17, just over five feet tall — pale, bespectacled, and heavily pregnant, with her long brown hair in a high bun. It was July 3, 2015, around 2 a.m. The two crept across the lawn to a small pale-gray trailer. Jace urged Brittany to stay outside, but she refused. He removed an air conditioner from the window, hoisted himself up, and then pulled her inside. She looked around: This had once been her room.

Sources indicate that together, they tiptoed toward the kitchen, past the pleather couch, the box TV, the grimy bathroom with its cracked tub, the piles of children’s clothing and toys, an old “Happy Birthday!” sign. Brittany and Jace headed to a door. Jace opened it and turned on the light. There, Robert “Robbie” Noce — balding, heavyset — was jolted from sleep. He sat up, disoriented. He gazed at Jace with confusion; they’d never met. As Jace shifted, Brittany came into view. A look of terror crossed Robbie’s face.

In a recent development, “Oh no, no, no,” he yelled. Jace moved toward Robbie, and the two began to tussle. Brittany approached as Jace pulled Robbie from the bed. Jace handed her a can of Axe cologne, and she sprayed Robbie in the face. “You ruined my life,” she yelled. “God doesn’t love you.”.

According to court documents and Brittany’s recollections, Jace held Robbie by the neck, trying to subdue him. Robbie reached for a large rechargeable battery. Brittany was fairly certain that Robbie hit Jace in the head with it. The two men fell to the ground.

Jace told Brittany to get him a knife and something to tie Robbie up with. She ran to the kitchen and grabbed the biggest knife. She saw a handful of ties and belts hanging on a door, handed them to Jace, and stepped into the bathroom. She could hear the sound of the knife tearing into Robbie’s skin and muscle, and she began to dry heave.
